activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
Charles had been in Japan for nine days, and he still could not make himself speak to his grandfather's photograph. It sat on a small altar in his aunt's house, framed in black, beside a bowl of rice that was refreshed each morning as though the dead man might still be hungry. The house smelled of incense and warm tatami. Charles's mother had shipped him here for the summer with the phrase "you should know that side of yourself," which he suspected was something adults said when they wanted a teenager out of the house but could not admit it. He had agreed anyway. His grandfather had died in March, three weeks before Charles was supposed to visit for the first time since he was four, and the visit had turned into a funeral and then a summer, and now he was here, in a country he half belonged to, mourning a man he could not remember.

His aunt was reticent in a way that confused him at first. She did not ask about his feelings. She asked whether he was eating, whether his futon was comfortable, whether he had found the fan in the closet. He mistook this for coldness until the third morning, when he came downstairs at six and found her crouched in the garden, building a small pyramid of kindling with a care he had only ever seen his mother use when wrapping presents.

"What is that?" he asked. The question came out wrong, too blunt, and he knew it.

She looked up at him, patient. "We light a fire at the beginning of Obon," she said. "To welcome the spirits home. Grandfather will find his way back to us by it."

He wanted to say something about combustion and carbon and the fact that dead people do not navigate, and he did not say it, because her hands were shaking slightly as she arranged the third stick. Later, walking to the river with her, he worked out that she had already had every skeptical thought he was having, probably decades of them, and had lit the fire anyway, every year, since her own grandmother died. He did not know what to do with that information. He titrated his silence carefully, saying nothing at home and asking the questions only in his head.

At the temple, the whole thing got louder. Monks chanted in a register that seemed to come up through the floorboards, and families crowded the halls with the particular patience of people who have done this annually forever. A boy near Charles's age, taller and louder, was arguing with a younger sister about who got to carry the lantern. Charles's mother would have called this boy "a lot." His aunt murmured that he was a cousin on the other side, from Nagoya, and that his grandmother had died the same winter as Charles's grandfather. The boy, whose name turned out to be barely pronounceable and therefore, in Charles's head, unnecessary, turned and said in English, "You're the American one. You carry one too. Everyone carries one."

"I don't know how," Charles said.

"You just hold it and don't drop it," the boy said, as though this were a complete philosophy. "My grandmother always said the hardest part is letting go at the end. That was her maxim. She thought she was funny." He did not look like he thought it was funny now.

They made the lanterns at long tables set up outside the temple gate, squares of paper stretched over bamboo frames, a candle set in the base. Charles wrote his grandfather's name in the careful katakana his aunt had taught him that morning, then added, in English, small enough that no one would read it, "I'm sorry I waited." The paintbrush was worse than a pen; the letters came out wobbling, and he had to accept that his apology would look, forever, like it had been written by a child. Somewhere behind him, the cousin was writing something long on his own lantern, shielding it with his arm, and Charles understood that grief made everyone secretive in their own dialect.

The river at dusk was crowded with people and with light. He had expected grief here to be quiet, but it was not; children ran along the bank, a grandmother laughed at something, monks moved among the families like unhurried referees. His aunt crouched at the water's edge, and Charles crouched beside her with his lantern, and she said, "The fires called them home at the beginning. Now the lanterns guide the spirits back. This is the last night of Obon." He understood, suddenly, the whole architecture of the week he had stumbled through: the fire at the beginning, the lantern at the end, the visit in between. You opened the door and you closed it, and both were love.

He set the lantern on the water and held the edge of it with two fingers, longer than he meant to, the paper going soft under his hands. The current pulled. His grandfather had wanted him to come for eleven years, had sent postcards Charles could not read, had once mailed him a baseball that sat on his shelf in Ohio with the wrapper still on. Charles had never written back. That was the fact he had been carrying all week, heavier than the lantern, and he could not put it on the water because it was not the kind of thing that floated.

"You can let it go now," his aunt said, not looking at him, looking at the current.

He let it go. The lantern caught the flow and joined the others, dozens of small lights turning slowly downstream like a procession that knew where it was going. The cousin's lantern passed his, the long message on its side unreadable in the dark, and the boy waded in past his ankles to watch it, not saying anything for the first time all day.

Charles's own light went under the bridge and out of sight, and he stayed crouched at the water's edge with his wet fingers, waiting to see if he would feel different, and the river just kept moving, indifferent and bright with everyone's lanterns, and his aunt put her hand briefly on his shoulder, once, like a period at the end of a sentence.

"Some of them make it all the way to the sea," the cousin said behind him, still watching the bridge. "Most of them tip over at the bend. My grandmother tipped over every year. She'd have hated that."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
The line outside the fire station ran along the curb and doubled back near the hydrant, and Victoria took her place behind a man in a hunting jacket who smelled of coffee and cold air. It was the first Tuesday after her eighteenth birthday, which she had marked on the calendar in gel pen weeks ago, the way other people marked exams. She had her driver's license in her coat pocket and her mother's opinions in one ear and her father's in the other, and the whole drive over she had been trying to work out what she actually thought.

Ahead of her in a different line, the shorter one that led to a folding table marked REGISTERED VOTERS ONLY, stood Lyam. She recognized the back of his head from civics, where he sat by the window and argued with the textbook more than with anybody else. He had moved here in September from Fargo. He was holding his license out to a poll worker, and the poll worker was shaking her head.

"You have to be on the rolls," the worker said. "You're not registered."

"That's the thing," Lyam said. "In North Dakota there's no voter registration at all. They abolished it in 1951. You just show up with your ID and vote. That's how it works there. My mom's voted in every election since the eighties and she's never registered once in her life."

The worker looked at him with the particular patience of someone who has heard many strange things before noon. "This isn't North Dakota."

"I know where I am," Lyam said. "I'm saying I didn't know I had to do anything in advance. Nobody told me there was a step."

Victoria watched him lower the license. Behind the table, sorting forms with quick hands, was Ms. Kim, who had taught her sophomore English and now apparently spent elections as a precinct officer. Ms. Kim caught her eye and raised one finger, meaning wait, meaning I see you. Victoria had always liked that about her, the way she could conduct an entire conversation in small gestures while doing three other things.

The line inched forward. The man in the hunting jacket put on reading glasses to study a sample ballot, and Victoria read over his shoulder, though she had already read hers at the kitchen table twice. Her mother wanted her to vote a straight ticket because principles only mattered if you won. Her father wanted her to split her ballot because a real citizen evaluates each candidate. For weeks Victoria had been trying to interpolate between them, plotting a course from one fixed point to the other, and the strange thing was that the line she drew never passed through either point. It wandered. It stopped at a school board candidate her mother had never heard of, and skipped a referendum her father considered obvious.

When she reached the front, Ms. Kim took her license, found her name, and had her sign. "First time," Ms. Kim said, not asking. She tore the corner off a sticker that said I VOTED and held it out. "The other one, your classmate. He can still vote. There's a same-day process, he just has to fill out a form. He's not disqualified, he's just from somewhere that does it differently." She said it quietly, angled away from Lyam's table, and Victoria understood she was not supposed to relay it as instruction from an authority but as something she had happened to overhear.

She carried her ballot to a booth with a short pencil on a string. The ballot was one page, two sides, and she filled in the ovals in the order she had decided at the kitchen table, not the order her parents would have chosen, and she did not feel the ground shift or the clouds part. She fed the page into the scanner, watched it swallow, and stood for a second in the open space between the booths and the door.

Lyam was still at the folding table, filling out the form with the same license propped in front of him like a witness. She walked over and put the sticker on his sleeve, pressing it flat with her thumb.

"For luck," she said. "North Dakota kid gets it done either way."

He looked down at the form, then up at her. "You're not going to tell me it's a painless process, are you?"

"It's interminable," she said. "Sign faster."

He laughed once through his nose and bent over the paper, and she watched the pen move, line by line, down the page.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of hot glue and orange juice, and by eight in the morning Carson had already rebuilt his poster board twice. His project sat on table fourteen: a demonstration of hydrogen combustion, complete with a small tank, a soap solution, and a speaker scheduled to go off between bubbles. The judges would begin their circuit at nine, and Mr. Tang, who taught chemistry and had a reputation for stopping at every single table, would want numbers. Numbers were the problem.

Carson had a card taped beside the tank where he'd transcribed his calculations from his notebook, and when he looked at it now, in the fluorescent light, something about it felt wrong in a way he couldn't name. He had written that burning four grams of hydrogen would produce four grams of water, because that seemed fair, mass going in equal to mass coming out. He'd doubled it for eight grams. He'd been proud of the arithmetic at one in the morning, less proud at eight.

Cale arrived at half past, carrying a stack of index cards for his own project two tables over, something about the diurnal activity of crickets, which he'd been recording on his phone for three weeks with a seriousness that surprised everyone who knew him. He leaned over Carson's card and squinted. "Where'd you get the grams?" he asked.

"I converted," Carson said. "Hydrogen's molar mass is about two, so four grams is two moles. Then I just matched it across."

"Matched what?"

"The water. Two moles of hydrogen makes two moles of water, so I said four grams of water." Saying it out loud made it worse. Cale picked up a marker from the table and held it out, handle first, like a man handing over a sword.

Down the row, Jamie was already at her table with a solar still, rehearsing under her breath in the rounded cadences of someone who had won the regional oratory prize last spring and had not let anyone forget it. When she wasn't performing, she spoke plainly, and Carson trusted the plain version more. He texted her: my numbers are wrong I think. grams of hydrogen to grams of water. help?

Her reply came before he'd put the phone down. Not grams. Moles don't weigh the same, that's the whole point. What's the equation?

He wrote it out on the back of Cale's cricket card: 2H2 + O2 goes to 2H2O. Then he counted, aloud, tapping the marker against each symbol. Two hydrogens per molecule of hydrogen gas, and the coefficient said two molecules, so four hydrogen atoms on the left. On the right, two molecules of water, each with two hydrogens, so four again. Same on both sides. "Okay," he said. "So two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen, and you get two moles of water out of it. That's what the equation is saying. Not two grams."

"Right," Jamie said, having appeared at his elbow without ceremony. "So start from your grams, get moles, use the equation, then go back to grams at the end. Water's molar mass is eighteen. Two moles of hydrogen gives you two moles of water, and two moles of water is thirty-six grams." She tapped his original card. "You were claiming four grams of hydrogen makes four grams of water. You were off by a whole oxygen."

He redid the card in fresh marker, each step on its own line: grams of hydrogen, divide by two to get moles, read the ratio straight off the balanced equation, multiply by eighteen. Eight grams of hydrogen, he now saw, would make seventy-two grams of water, not eight. The mass came from somewhere; it had just never occurred to him to ask where. He was still not entirely sure he could explain, under pressure, why the oxygen's mass joined the party so invisibly, and he wrote a small note in the corner reminding himself to say "from the oxygen" if a judge pressed him.

The doors opened at nine. Mr. Tang came to table fourteen first, as predicted, read the card top to bottom, and pointed at the bubble solution. "Light one," he said. Carson squeezed the bulb, raised a single trembling soap sphere, and touched the candle to it. The pop cracked through the gym, small and bright, and a scatter of water droplets landed on the poster board, darkening the ink of the last line. Mr. Tang put one finger near the spot. "Condensed product," he said, almost to himself, and moved on down the row toward the crickets.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
story:
The city hall study room smelled of floor wax and old carpet, and Jeremy had claimed the corner table an hour before anyone else arrived because the light there was good and the radiator actually worked. He spread his notes across the surface like a man defending territory: a diagram of Westminster on the left, one of Washington on the right, and between them a blank space he kept staring at as if it owed him money.

Santino dropped into the opposite chair with a coffee he had clearly not bought for himself, given the name scrawled on the cup. "Lennox is parking. He says the garage is a stratum of hell we haven't discovered yet." He peered at the diagrams. "Which one is which?"

"The one with the crown on it is Britain."

"Very helpful."

Lennox arrived complaining about the garage, then about the elevator, then about a pigeon that had apparently looked at him with intent. He sat, saw the diagrams, and groaned. "Mr. Nguyen is going to ask me to explain confidence conventions again, isn't he."

"He asks everyone," Jeremy said. "That's the whole point of the review session. He rents the room from the city every year. Says it makes the test feel civic."

It was true that Mr. Nguyen had booked the study room at city hall for the weekend before the exam, an arrangement that struck Jeremy as either charming or slightly mad. The room had a portrait of a former mayor whose expression suggested permanent disappointment, and a plaque about a drainage project from 1974. Lennox said the plaque was the most honest thing in the building.

They worked through it. In the parliamentary system, the head of government was chosen by the legislature, which meant the same body could remove him with a vote of no confidence, and Jeremy drew an arrow to show it, then a second arrow going back, because after a government fell there was usually another election or another attempt at forming a government, and the whole thing looped like a water slide. In the presidential system, the president was elected separately, for a fixed term, and could only be removed through impeachment, which was harder, more formal, and rarer. Jeremy wrote "recalcitrant" beside the impeachment box and underlined it twice, then wondered if that was showing off and reduced it to one underline.

"So the prime minister can just be fired," Santino said, chewing his pen. "By his own people. Any Tuesday."

"Basically."

"That's terrifying."

"That's the trade," Jeremy said. "Flexibility versus stability. The Americans locked their arrangement down on purpose so it wouldn't ossify around one guy. Like the term limit thing."

Lennox looked up. "What term limit thing?"

Jeremy tapped his notes. He had copied the fact from his textbook the night before, because it had surprised him, and he liked being the one who had it. "The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution. Ratified in 1951. It limits a person to being elected president twice."

"Twelve years," Santino said.

"Twice," Jeremy said. "Two elections. It's not the same if you take over mid-term, but the amendment says twice elected. I'm not going further than that because that's all I wrote down."

Lennox frowned at the ceiling. "Why, though? If a president is popular, why can't he just keep running?"

"Because after Roosevelt they decided they didn't want anyone becoming permanent," Jeremy said, and then stopped, because that was the textbook's phrase and he wasn't sure he could defend it if pressed. "I mean, that's the history I have. The point for the exam is that a parliamentary system doesn't need that rule, since the legislature can pull the plug whenever it wants. The Americans needed a hard limit because their removal mechanism is so stiff."

"So you're saying one system trusts the politicians and the other trusts the rules."

"I'm saying one system makes removal easy and cheap, and the other makes it hard and rare, and each of those costs something." Jeremy turned his pen end over end. "The vote of no confidence can topple a government over something petty. Impeachment is so heavy it basically never lands. Which one is better depends on what you're afraid of."

Santino wrote that down word for word, which made Jeremy uneasy, because he didn't entirely believe it himself. There was a case, he thought, for the parliamentary way being more honest, since it admitted that confidence was political, but there was also a case that a country deserved intervals, fixed and predictable, where the leader couldn't be churned out mid-stride. He had gone back and forth for two days and had settled, provisionally, on liking each system for the failure it prevented rather than the success it produced, and he suspected that position was a way of not choosing.

The door opened and Mr. Nguyen came in carrying a folding easel under one arm and a bag of clementines, which he set on the table like a peace offering. "Good, you're early. The radiator works in here? Last year I froze with the AP comparative class and we all pretended it was character-building." He surveyed their diagrams, his eyes moving from Westminster to Washington and stopping at the blank space between. "And this gap is?"

"The part I can't fill," Jeremy said.

"Good," said Mr. Nguyen, peeling a clementine. "Leave it empty. It means you understand the size of the question." He turned to the whiteboard and uncapped a marker. "Now. Someone explain to me how each system removes its head of government, and Lennox, I'm sorry, but this year it's you."

Lennox stared at his diagram, at the arrows, at the word he had watched Jeremy underline. Santino slid his coffee an inch toward him, a gesture of either sympathy or ransom. Mr. Nguyen waited, marker poised, and outside, in the plaza, a flag rope clinked against its pole.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search works only on sorted data: it compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half of the list that cannot contain it.
story:
The programming club met in the library's back room every Thursday, which meant that by six o'clock the smell of old paper had blended with instant noodles, and tonight it also meant the clock on the wall was an enemy. The county coding contest closed submissions at nine, and their club project, a program that looked up member names in the robotics team roster, was failing in a way nobody could explain.

"It skips people," Keven said, spinning his chair in slow circles. "I typed in Devi, nothing. I typed in Chen, nothing. But Alonso works, and Bianchi works. It likes the beginning of the alphabet and holds a grudge against the rest."

Simran leaned over his laptop, chewing a pen cap. "Maybe it's political. Your code has opinions."

"My code is elegant," Keven said, and then began to pontificate about loops, about how his algorithm was too refined for the clumsy roster, about how in a just world his genius would be recognized without debugging. Stella let him run down like a music box. She pulled the laptop toward her instead, and behind them Mr. Szabó, the librarian, paused his cart of returns to watch over her shoulder with the polite patience of a magistrate waiting for a witness to get to the point.

Stella read the function twice. She had seen the pattern before, or something like it. Last summer, hunting for a particular volume of poetry, she had stood in front of the S shelves while Mr. Szabó told her not to check every single spine like a tired tourist. Start in the middle, he had said; see what you find there, and if it comes after what you want, ignore everything to the right. She had found Szymborska in three moves instead of forty and had felt, briefly, like a magician. Keven's code was doing the same trick, she realized: it went to the middle of the list, compared, and threw away the half that couldn't hold the answer. That was why it was fast. That was the whole swagger of it.

"Wait," she said. "The trick only works if the list is sorted."

"It is sorted," Keven said.

"By whom?"

He opened his mouth, then closed it. Simran scrolled to the roster file, and there it all was, names typed in the order people had signed up at the club fair: Nakamura, Alvarez, Okafor, Bianchi, Devi, Chen. Nobody had ever sorted it, because nobody had thought a list needed tending, like a garden nobody watered. Stella laughed, and then tried not to, and then gave up.

"So it goes to the middle, finds Nakamura, decides Devi must be in the left half because the middle comes after D," she said, tapping the screen, "and throws the right half away. Except Devi is sitting in the right half, laughing at us."

"Betrayed by my own elegance," Keven said. "This is the tragedy of my life."

"Fix it and submit," Simran said. "Twenty minutes for the upload, and I still have to write the team description." She was being effusive about the roster fix in a way that struck Stella as slightly strategic, since Simran had been the one assigned to type in the names, but Stella let that go too. There was a cleaner justice available: fix it, submit it, tease later.

Stella added one line that put the list in order before the search ran, then typed Devi into the box. The name came back in an instant, match found, and behind them Mr. Szabó said "ha" softly, the way a man says it when he has watched someone learn a thing he hinted at months ago and never explained. Chen worked. Okafor worked. Keven tested every name twice, muttering apologies to each one like a magistrate reversing wrongful convictions.

At 8:52 the confirmation banner came up, entry received, and Simran raised her noodle cup in salute while Keven bowed from his chair, nearly tipping over. Stella saved a second copy of the file to a USB drive, because eight minutes was enough time to become cautious, and then sat back and looked at the one line of sorting code that had cost them an evening.

"Next year we sort first," she said. "Actually, next year we test first."

"Next year," Keven said, "the roster comes to me pre-sorted, or I don't code."

Simran slurped her noodles. "I'll type it in alphabetical order, and then we can all sit here with nothing to fix."

"Deal," Stella said, and pulled the USB drive from the slot.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle.
story:
The community hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged in a horseshoe with the gap facing a plywood podium. Florence had claimed the seat nearest the outlet because her phone was at four percent, which she recognized, standing there, was part of the problem she'd been asked to argue. Ms. Whitehead had assigned sides by drawing names from a coffee tin, and Florence had drawn against Caleigh, who wanted, with a ferocity Florence usually admired, to prove that ancient rules were ancient and that was the end of it.

"Switching on a phone," Caleigh said during the first cross-examination, "is not plowing a field. It's not kindling a fire in a desert. It's a rectangle in your pocket." The audience of eleven, mostly classmates who had come for the free pizza, laughed at the right moment. Benny, timing the rounds on his watch, held up two fingers to signal that Florence had two minutes left, and she spent the first thirty seconds of them watching Caleigh's confident posture and understanding, with a small sinking, that she had prepared for a different debate than the one happening.

She had prepared by actually reading. Not the summaries Caleigh had quoted, which cited scholars citing other scholars, but the source itself, in a library edition with a cracked spine, the night before, eating cold pizza over the kitchen table while her mother asked whether this was for a grade. What she'd found was that the Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle. Thirty-nine, not ten, not a vague cloud of piety. Categories, which meant the list was meant to delimit something, to mark a boundary rather than drown people in prohibition.

"So it's a fence," Caleigh said when Florence raised it. "A fence around a fence. My point exactly."

"It's a lemma," Florence said. She hadn't planned to say the word; it had come to her at two in the morning, reading. "A stepping-stone. You take the categories, you ask what the category was for, and then you ask whether the phone is inside it." She moved away from the podium, which Ms. Whitehead allowed because the rules of this club were loose. "One of the categories is kindling fire. Is a circuit closing a kind of kindling? Old rabbis argued about walking on grass, about a sandal, about carrying a needle. They weren't done deciding. That's the part that surprises people. The rule isn't finished."

Benny's watch beeped. The hall's radiator clanked the way it did every evening, and someone's paper cup rolled off a chair and made a small hollow sound on the floor.

Caleigh's rebuttal was good, Florence had to admit it was good even as her ears went hot. Caleigh said that a rule which needs a scholar to tell you what it means has already failed the person it's for, that her grandmother had kept the Sabbath in a riparian village where the river carried all the work away on Saturdays and nobody had needed a list, and that love of a rule was not the same as the rule being right. Florence stood at the podium for her final statement and found that she agreed with about half of it, which was, she discovered in real time, a catastrophic position to hold in a debate and possibly the only honest one.

She said so. She said the list was built from the Tabernacle, a thing made once, for a purpose, and that a phone was also a thing made for a purpose, and that the question of whether the purposes were alike was a question the text itself could not close. She said the rabbis had linked the 39 categories to the work of building, and that this made the Sabbath not a list of nos but a weekly argument about what work is for. Then she lost. Benny read the cards: seven to four, Caleigh, and Caleigh did a small, contained victory gesture that Florence would think about later, on the walk home, more than she thought about the loss itself.

Afterward, Caleigh helped stack the chairs, not looking at Florence, and Ms. Whitehead gathered the coffee tin and said, quietly, that Florence's second rebuttal had been the best speech in the room and it had also been the reason she'd lost. Florence carried the last two chairs to the wall. Her phone had died during the final round, screen gone black on the folding table, and she stood a moment with her thumb resting on the button without pressing it. Caleigh zipped her bag, paused at the door, and said, "Same time next month?" Florence's thumb was still on the button.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose.
story:
Cameron had cleared the coffee table down to one legal pad and a pen with a bitten cap, and he had been sitting in his living room for forty minutes without writing anything that survived. The assignment from Ms. Tremblay was simple enough to say aloud and enormous to do: a ten-minute play, staged in class, drawn from a moment in your own life. The couch cushion under him still held the shape of his father, who was on furlough from the plant and had taken to watching daytime television in this room until Cameron exiled both the television and his father to the kitchen with a politeness that had taken negotiation. Now the room was quiet in the late afternoon way, dust turning slowly in the window light, and the legal pad held three abandoned openings, each crossed out with a single decisive line that he regretted immediately after drawing it.

The trouble was the subject. He had a moment, the real one, the one that kept surfacing whenever he let his mind go slack: his older sister on the back steps last spring, telling him she was not going back to school in the fall, and him saying nothing clever, nothing kind, only "okay," and then carrying the garbage to the curb so he would have somewhere to put his hands. He wanted to write that. He also did not want to put her in a play and hand it to Sidney and Izabelle and a room of classmates, because a play is not a diary; a play gets acted, out loud, by people who will look at the girl who is not his sister and then look at him.

He had invited Sidney over partly for this, and Sidney arrived at five with a bag of chips and no ceremony, dropping onto the far end of the couch and reading the crossed-out openings upside down without asking. "You're stalling," Sidney said.

"I'm deciding who it's about."

"It's about your sister. Obviously." Sidney crumpled the chip bag into the space between them. "That's the whole reason it's good and the whole reason you won't write it."

Cameron told him about the spring semester English unit instead of answering, how Ms. Tremblay had passed out The Glass Menagerie in those diaphanous yellow used-bookstore copies, the kind that seem about to dissolve in your hands. He had read the introduction late one night, past the part where he was supposed to stop, and found the sentence he now recited from memory because he had gone back to it three times: Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in the play, on his own sister Rose. He said it plainly, without commentary, and watched Sidney take it in.

"So he did it," Sidney said. "He put his actual sister on the stage and changed her name."

"He did more than change her name. He made her glass animals and a limp and a gentleman caller who never comes back. He made her Laura." Cameron stood and moved the lamp so the light fell across the pad, a small governing action that made him feel briefly like someone with a plan. "That's the part I keep circling. He didn't just hide her. He translated her. And I can't tell if that's an act of love or an act of theft, and I've been sitting here for an hour pretending the answer will arrive if I wait."

Izabelle came at six, because he had texted her, and she sat on the floor with her back against the armchair and made him say the whole back-steps moment out loud, once, without the legal pad. He gave it to her in the flat voice of a police report: the steps, the season, the word "okay," the garbage. She was quiet after, and then she said, "In your version she's already decided. That's not how it happened, is it. You don't actually know what she'd decided." That had not occurred to him, and it desiccate(d) his comfortable version of the scene right there on the table, left it dry and weightless, because she was right: he had written his own silence into her mouth, given her certainty so that his "okay" would have something to push against.

He wrote for twenty minutes while Izabelle read a magazine and Sidney ate the last of the chips and offered no opinion. What came out was a scene between a brother and a sister named Marcia, on steps he made concrete instead of their steps, in a town he made up, and Marcia said things his sister had never said, and the brother still said only "okay," because that part he could not and would not change. He did not know yet whether the play would be any good, or whether Marcia was a respectful translation or a borrowed body, or whether his sister, if she ever sat in an audience and watched a stranger play her, would recognize herself in the diaphanous distance between the fact and the invention. He read the last page over once, and Izabelle looked up from her magazine, and he said, "Marcia gets the second-to-last line. She gets to answer him."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Morgan's grandmother had sent the photo at 6:14 in the morning, which was her way of saying good morning: a flooded street, a man on a roof holding a dog, and a caption in enormous letters about how the whole city was underwater. By lunch, half the school seemed to have it too. Maksim slid his phone across the cafeteria table toward Morgan and Audrina with the tenderness of a man presenting evidence in court.

"This," he said, "is my ticket to actually winning the journalism feature Ms. Fortin keeps saying I haven't written. Breaking coverage of the flood."

"What flood?" Audrina said. "It rained yesterday. My shoes are still damp. That's the extent of the disaster."

"The flood in the picture, Audrina. The catastrophic one." Maksim turned the phone around and frowned at it himself, as if it had already started to disappoint him.

Morgan had the same photo on her own phone, sitting above her grandmother's message, "Is your school okay?? Call me," and she had spent her morning not calling but wondering. The man on the roof looked familiar in a way she couldn't place. So did the dog, honestly, though she recognized that dogs on roofs form a kind of universal category. There was something off about the light, and the cars parked along the drowned street had a boxy, old-fashioned shape, like the cars from the movie her grandmother paused every twenty minutes to explain.

"Before you write a feature," she said, "maybe find out when it happened. You know you can search a picture itself? Like, put the image in and it finds where else it shows up."

Maksim looked at her with the flat distrust of a person being told the floor is lava. "You made that up."

"I didn't. It's been a thing since 2011. You upload the picture or paste its link, and it finds other places it appears on the web." Morgan took his phone, opened the search engine, and started hunting for the little camera icon in the search box, feeling oddly like a safecracker who had only read about safes.

"How do you even know that?" Audrina asked, leaning over her shoulder.

"My grandmother sends me a dramatic photo approximately every eleven days. At some point you develop survival skills." She found the icon, dragged the image in, and hit enter. The results bloomed up the screen: the same flooded street, the same dog, on pages dated years ago. One page, in a language that used a whole different alphabet, had transliterated the caption into Latin characters underneath, and Morgan squinted at it, sounding out the words like a kindergartner, while Audrina provided unhelpful phonetic commentary from the side. "There was a flood," Morgan said finally. "Somewhere. Once. Not here, and not this week, and this dog has been famous for years."

"Wait," Audrina said. "This dog is famous?"

"The dog is a legend," Morgan said. "There are whole pages about this dog."

Maksim took his phone back slowly, the way you take back a pet that has done something embarrassing. He scrolled through the results in silence, and Morgan watched his feature story visibly evaporate. "So there's no flood," he said.

"There's no flood. There was a flood, past tense, in a different country, before either of us could walk. If you post this you'll be the guy who reported a decade-old flood on a street that's probably fine."

"Probably a nice street," Audrina offered. "The cars were cute."

Ms. Fortin found them like that at the end of lunch, three phones crowded over one ruined scoop, and asked what they were investigating. Maksim, who could never resist an authority figure with a clipboard, explained the whole thing at twice the necessary speed: the photo, the grandmother, the search, the dog's improbable fame. "So I have no story," he finished. "Unless."

"Unless," Ms. Fortin said, "the story is a flooded street that fooled three hundred people in one cafeteria, and how one of them checked it before forwarding it to three hundred more."

Morgan hadn't thought of it as anything, really, just the thing you did instead of being the granddaughter who forwarded nonsense back to her grandmother. But Maksim was already writing the lede in his head; she could see it in his face, the particular gleam of a boy who has found a way to lose and win at the same time. He turned out to be impervious to disappointment the way certain people are impervious to weather, which was probably why he'd survive journalism. "You'll be my source," he told Morgan. "Quote one. 'I just didn't want my grandmother to think my school was underwater.'"

"You are not quoting me as saying that."

"Quote two: 'The dog is a legend.'"

That evening, Morgan sat on her bed and called her grandmother, who answered on the first ring, delighted, already mid-sentence about the water level. Morgan held the phone loosely in one hand and turned her own screen toward the ceiling light, the search box open, the little camera waiting. "Grandma," she said. "Do you have five minutes? I want to show you something about that dog."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The stadium smelled like burnt pretzels and cold air, and Savannah had never been anywhere so loud. Her father had won the tickets through work, four of them in the last row of the lower bowl, and her grandfather had refused to let them go unused even though the walk from the parking lot had taken him twenty minutes and two rests. Between them sat Santiago, who had brought a foam finger he was too embarrassed to wear, and Holly, who was live-texting the game to her cousin in Halifax.

The home team was down two goals halfway through the second period, and the crowd had gone from celebration to something more like litigation, everyone arguing their case to the referees in advance. Savannah's grandfather leaned toward her during a commercial break and said the ice was better in the old days, which was the adage he produced for every occasion, and which she had long ago stopped trying to fact-check. It was hard to know what he remembered and what he had renovated.

"Tell them the trophy thing," her father said, nudging him. "Savannah's doing a history project. She'll appreciate it."

Her grandfather straightened. "The Stanley Cup," he said, "was donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston. First awarded in 1893. Oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America." He recited it the way other men recited psalms, and Savannah, who had assumed the fact was a family myth the way his claim of having once shaken Jean Béliveau's hand was a family myth, typed it into her phone under the escalator lights. The whole thing checked out. Every number. She felt oddly betrayed by its being true.

"The trophy is older than the league," Santiago said, reading over her shoulder. "That's insane. It's like the cup rented out the NHL as a delivery service."

Holly was less impressed. "It's a cup," she said. "People lionize a cup. My cousin in Halifax has a cup with a trophy in it from darts, 1987, and nobody builds a hall of fame around that one."

"Because your cousin's dart trophy is spartan," Santiago said, gesturing at the dome where the banners hung. "This one has a hall of fame. That's the difference between a thing and a legend."

"It's still a cup you drink out of," Holly said, and Savannah's grandfather, who had not followed any of this, said happily, "They drink out of it. The winners. That's the whole point," as though Holly had agreed with him.

The home team scored twice in the third period to tie it, and the noise became physical, a pressure against Savannah's eardrums she could feel in her teeth. During overtime her grandfather took out his phone, the ancient one with the cracked screen, and showed her a photograph: a much younger him, in a coat with lapels like dinner plates, standing beside a display case. "There," he said. "I told you. Béliveau." Savannah looked at the photo, at the tall man in the case's reflection who was very possibly nobody, and at her grandfather's face, which was waiting. She had spent the drive here rehearsing what she would say about the project, about how she'd decided the trophy was really a kind of civic lie people agreed to tell, how old things mattered because they were old and for no better reason, and that she was honest enough to admit she couldn't decide whether that was beautiful or a trick. She had a whole paragraph of it in her notes.

Instead she said, "Can I use this?"

He handed the phone over like it was a ring. "Borrow it. Copy it. I have the original at home, from before everything was phones."

When the winning goal came, four minutes into the second overtime, nobody in her row saw it live. Her father was standing with his back to the ice, arguing with a man one row down about a line change that had happened in 2011. Santiago had his foam finger raised in the wrong direction. Holly was mid-text, thumb frozen, her cousin in Halifax about to receive a message that ended forever in the middle of the word "sa." Only the grandfather saw it, and he was already crying, quietly, before the horns finished, holding his phone against his chest with both hands.

Savannah took his picture like that, and then, because the crowd was moving and no one would notice, one more of the ice, where the players were piling on each other in front of a net she couldn't quite see.

"Send me the Béliveau one," she shouted over the noise, and he shouted back, "You'll have to come get it, I don't know how," and Holly grabbed her sleeve and pointed at the scoreboard, where the word CHAMPIONS was repeating itself in gold.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
The garage smelled of cut aluminum and the ghost of his father's cologne, which had outlasted the man himself by most of a year. Cohen had two sheets of foil stapled to a frame of scrap wood, a length of wax paper between them, and a multimeter borrowed from the school, and by Sunday night he needed to be able to explain all of it to a judge at the regional science fair.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Maksim said from the workbench, where he was supposedly sanding the display board. Maksim had signed on as Cohen's assistant because his own project, an attempt to grow crystals in his mother's pressure cooker, had ended in a smell that cleared the kitchen for two days.

"It's a capacitor," Cohen said. "Two plates, charge on each. The fair booklet wants the field strength between the plates, not just the charge. I don't know how to get it."

Lisa arrived with her bike helmet still on and a grocery bag of batteries, because she had decided, without anyone asking, that the project needed more power. She set the bag down and looked at the foil sheets with an expression that suggested she was already reorganizing them in her mind.

"So what do you know," she said.

"Voltage across the plates. Distance between them. That's what I can measure."

She flipped the batteries out of the bag one at a time, lining them up on the bench like a jury. "Then measure both and stop suffering."

He clipped the meter leads to the plates, read the voltage, then took a ruler to the gap. Twelve volts, three centimeters. Somewhere in the garage's cluttered silence, Maksim was pretending not to listen, which for Maksim was a form of listening.

The school's physics book was in Cohen's backpack, and he got it out and sat on the cold concrete floor with it, running his finger down the chapter on fields. He found it between two paragraphs he half-remembered: between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them. E equals V over d. He read it three times, because it seemed too easy, like being told a river's speed was the drop divided by the length.

"So," Lisa said, watching him over the display board. She had commandeered the sander from Maksim and was doing the actual work. "What's the field."

"Voltage divided by distance," Cohen said. "That's all it is. V over d."

"Show off," Maksim said, with feeling.

Cohen did the arithmetic in the margin of the booklet. Twelve divided by three hundredths, four hundred volts per meter. He said the number out loud and felt an unfamiliar exhilaration, the specific kind that comes from a machine finally doing what the paper promised. He'd built something and then predicted it with a sentence, and the two had agreed.

The trouble started when he checked it. He moved the plates closer, to two centimeters, expecting a bigger number, and the meter barely changed, which meant the field should have jumped, and it did, six hundred, but the voltage shouldn't have sat still like that with his battery stack sagging. He tore the setup apart twice. Lisa watched the second time, arms crossed, helmet finally off, and the subtext of her posture was clear enough even to him: she thought he was being dramatic.

"It's not drama," he said. "It's either wrong or it's telling me something."

Maksim, who had gone very quiet near the bench, cleared his throat. He confessed in the manner of a man pleading indigent before a magistrate, offering nothing but circumstance. He had swapped the school's meter for his uncle's, because he'd been afraid Cohen would damage the good one, and his uncle's meter had a dial setting he hadn't understood. The readings had been in millivolts all along, which meant the voltage was a thousandth of what they thought, which meant the field was too, and every number Cohen had written on the display board was beautiful, coherent and wrong.

Lisa started laughing first, then couldn't stop, then hugged the display board to keep from sliding off the stool. Cohen sat on the floor again with the book and the borrowed meter and started over, because the sentence was still true even if they were not.

Monday, in the school gymnasium, the third judge to reach his table was Ms. Saleh, who had given him a B-minus on a lab report in the fall and a look that said she remembered it. She picked up his capacitor, turned it over, and asked how he'd found the field between the plates.

"Voltage divided by distance," Cohen said. "E equals V over d."

She looked at him for a long moment, the way she'd looked at the lab report.

"And the meter this time," she said, tapping the school's own, sitting squarely on his table, "reads actual volts?"

"Yes," Cohen said, and slid his data sheet toward her.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers.
story:
The bus smelled of synthetic orange and cold coffee, and Connor had spent the ride with his forehead against the window, watching the tech campus assemble itself out of glass the way a photograph develops. Ms. Asante had given them lanyards and one instruction: ask a real question, not a polite one. He had a real question folded in his notebook, though he'd been arguing with himself about whether it was a good one or an ungrateful one, since his father had pulled a second shift to afford the trip's deposit and the campus tour had a table of free pens.

A guide with a practiced laugh led them through an atrium where a screen taller than a doorway displayed a map of data flows, animated arrows pulsing between cities. Alistair hung back beside Connor, arms crossed, wearing the expression he saved for things that impressed him against his will. Abigayle walked ahead, phone out, photographing everything, which was her way of owning it.

"Here's where we test the hiring models," the guide said, stopping at a lab of empty desks. "The algorithm learns from our past recruiters, so it can screen a thousand applications in the time a person screens ten."

"Does it inherit their mistakes?" Connor asked. The question came out flatter than he'd rehearsed it.

The guide smiled. "It's a tool. Tools are neutral."

Alistair snorted. "A hammer built by a biased carpenter still hits crooked."

"That's not how it works," the guide said, but a woman at the far desk, wearing a badge and no smile, looked up from her monitor and kept looking, and Connor filed the look away.

The second room was worse and more interesting. A wall of monitors showed the lobby they'd passed through forty minutes earlier, the cafeteria, a stairwell. Abigayle leaned toward her own image, grainy, small, holding her phone.

"So what," she said. "I've got nothing to hide. I'm seventeen. My life is calculus and group chats."

Alistair turned. "Would you mind a list of everyone you call?"

She blinked. "Like, a contact list?"

"Like a list someone else keeps. Every number, how long you talked."

Connor stepped in, because he'd been waiting for this without knowing it. "That's not hypothetical," he said. "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden showed the NSA was collecting phone records, numbers called, call durations, from millions of Verizon customers."

Abigayle's thumb stopped moving on her phone. "Millions of regular people."

"Who weren't suspects," Connor said. "Just customers."

The guide cleared his throat. "That was lawful under a court order, and it's history now."

"Is it?" Alistair said. "This wall here, is that history?"

"The company is transparent about it. There's signage in the lobby."

"There is," Abigayle said slowly, and Connor watched her turn her own argument over, examining its underside. "I signed a form at the door. I read the first two lines."

Ms. Asante had drifted to the back of the group, and she said nothing, which Connor understood as its own kind of instruction. He thought about his father's second shift, and about the pens, and about how gratitude could be used like a lock, and he thought too that the guide might genuinely believe what he was saying, that probity and convenience could share a desk. Maybe they could. That was the part he couldn't resolve, standing there.

In the lobby, at the exit, there was a station where visitors could request their own surveillance data, a compliance gesture, a small kiosk with an ascetic little interface, white screen, one button. Alistair walked past it. Abigayle stopped, then didn't press it, then stopped again.

The woman with no smile came down the stairwell and cut through the group. "You asked about the hiring model," she said to Connor, quietly enough that the guide couldn't quite claim the conversation. "It inherited the old recruiters' patterns. We know. I flagged it twice." She pressed a printed slip into his hand. "There's a public comment window closing Friday. A comment on the record can't exculpate any of us, but it can slow a rollout."

Connor looked at the slip. A URL, a deadline, a case number.

Abigayle pressed the button at the kiosk. A message thanked her for her request and said her data would arrive within thirty days. She stared at the screen as if expecting more, and when nothing came, she photographed the message itself, flash glaring off the glass.

On the bus, Ms. Asante collected the lanyards one by one. When she took Connor's, she saw the slip in his other hand and held his gaze a moment longer than the transaction required.

"You'll comment," she said. It was not a question, and it was not permission either.

Connor looked out the window at the campus receding, its glass giving back the afternoon sun so that the whole building became a flat bright field, unreadable. He folded the slip along its crease and put it in his notebook, between two pages, where the weight of the pen he'd taken would hold it flat.

Abigayle slid into the seat across the aisle. "Thirty days," she said. "You think they'll actually send it?"

"Friday," Connor said. "The comment closes Friday."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole.
story:
The kitchen scale was supposed to be Seth's mother's diet scale, and it was supposed to measure grams, and it was supposed to work. It flickered between 146.1 and 146.2 as he stood over it with a bag of table salt, pencil behind his ear like a carpenter in a movie he'd half watched once.

"You look like a dour little chemist," said Lyle from the doorway, already stealing a granola bar from the cupboard. "The science fair is Thursday, right? You're going to stand there frowning at salt until then?"

"I'm not frowning. I'm concentrating. There's a difference, and one of them gets results." Seth set the bag down and the scale settled on 146.10 grams. "The problem is my experiment needs two moles of sodium chloride, and I don't know how much two moles weighs, because I zoned out during the exact week Mr. Fernando taught that part."

Lyle leaned against the counter, chewing. "So ask him."

"I did ask him. That's the worst part." Seth pulled a folded sheet from his pocket and smoothed it on the table. "I asked him after class and he said, and I quote, 'You could ask Isabela, or you could reason it out,' and then he walked away like a man who has abrogated all responsibility for my education."

"Harsh."

"He said it kindly, though. That's the thing about him. Even his refusals come with a little bow." Seth tapped the paper, where he'd copied a number from the textbook's back page: sodium chloride has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole. He'd written it in his neatest handwriting, which meant it was legible to roughly one person on earth, himself.

Lyle squinted at it. "So what does that even mean, molar mass?"

"It means, I think, that one mole weighs 58.44 grams. Like how a dozen eggs weighs a certain amount, except a mole is the chemist's dozen, except it's an insane number of things instead of twelve." Seth was already dividing on paper. "So if one mole is 58.44 grams, then two moles is twice that. 116.88 grams."

"That sounds suspiciously like multiplication."

"It's the only part of this I trust." Seth measured out 116.88 grams of salt into a bowl, apologizing silently to the scale for doubting it earlier. The salt made a soft white cone with a depression in the middle, like a tiny volcano that had given up.

His phone buzzed. A message from Isabela: "Mr. F told me you asked about moles. Don't buy anything. He also said your bag problem was 'a good puzzle,' which from him means he's enjoying watching you suffer. Do you actually have it or are you guessing?"

Seth typed back: "I have it. 116.88 grams for two moles. The bag is 146.10, so there's more than enough, and now I even know how many moles are in the whole bag if I divide. But here's my problem: is the molar mass thing exactly right, or close? The book says 'about.'"

There was a long pause, long enough that Lyle started narrating. "She's typing. She stopped. She's typing again. She's gone to get a snack, I bet."

The reply came: "About 58.44, which is close enough for anything you'd do at a science fair, unless your project is 'measuring salt with impossible precision,' in which case, why? Also your division: 146.10 divided by 58.44. Do it and tell me what you get, because I got a weird number and I want to know if we match."

Seth worked it out on the paper, tongue between his teeth. 146.10 divided by 58.44 came to something just under two and a half. "2.49," he sent. "So the whole bag is about 2.5 moles. Isabela, what did you get?"

"2.499," she wrote back. "We match. Congrats, you reasoned it out, exactly like Mr. Fernando wanted, and I only helped a little, which is apparently his favorite amount. Also he's standing behind me in the library and he read this whole conversation over my shoulder, so, you know, wave to the camera."

Lyle laughed so hard he had to set down the granola bar. "He's the most ascetic man alive and he's still reading your texts like a gossip."

"He's not ascetic, he owns a boat."

"He owns a small boat and wears the same four shirts. That's boat-themed asceticism."

Seth looked at the bowl of salt, the paper, the number 116.88 circled twice. He still wasn't certain why a mole was defined the way it was, or why the molar mass was "about" 58.44 rather than exactly, and he suspected there was a reason that would show up in some later chapter and ambush him. But the salt was measured, the bag was enough, and the arithmetic had survived Isabela, which was more than most of his arithmetic could say.

He tipped the measured salt carefully into a jar and labeled it with a marker: TWO MOLES, ALLEGEDLY.

"Allegedly?" Lyle said.

"Every good claim deserves a little doubt," Seth said, and screwed the lid on tight.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
story:
The pond behind the library had one good bench, and Alexia had claimed it by arriving at seven, before Kasey and Noelle finished their shift at the grocery store. Her biology test was at nine the next morning, which meant she had roughly one day to understand how DNA became protein, a process Mr. Wu had described on the board as transcription and translation before the bell cut him off. She had a textbook, a phone with no signal at this end of the park, and a half-edited video on her laptop that she was supposed to finish for the media elective by Friday. Both deadlines pressed on her at once, and the water moved slowly in front of her, indifferent to either.

She had made the video for the elective, a short documentary about the pond, and it was full of bad takes. There was the minute where a dog had run through the frame, the stretch where she had said "um" eleven times, the part where a goose had honked over her whole explanation of the turtles. Editing meant cutting all of that out and joining the good pieces so the video flowed, and she had been at it long enough that evening that the work had begun to feel like dreaming.

Kasey arrived first, dropping onto the far end of the bench with a bag of chips. "Tell me you know what introns are," Kasey said. "Because I read the chapter twice and it's like the words slide off."

"I know some of it," Alexia said. "DNA gets copied into RNA first. That part's transcription. Then the RNA gets read to build a protein. That's translation." She had the sequence, at least. What she did not have was any sense of why the chapter spent two full pages on what happens to the RNA in between.

Noelle came down the path with her own textbook held open like a tray, reading while she walked, which she could apparently do without stepping in the water. "Okay, so, this is the part I hate," she said, sitting on the grass. "The RNA gets made, and it's a mess, and then it gets fixed somehow. The chapter uses all these words. Splicing. Introns. Exons. I keep losing the thread."

Alexia looked at her laptop screen, where the timeline of her documentary ran along the bottom in a long strip. She had just highlighted the goose honk, a jagged spike in the audio, and cut it, then dragged the two clean sections together so that her narration continued without a gap. She sat very still.

"Wait," she said. She cut the dog minute. She dragged. She cut the "ums," one by one, and pulled the remaining pieces until they touched. The video played through smooth and continuous, as though the dog had never crossed the frame at all.

"That's it," she said. "That's what happens to the RNA. In plant and animal cells, the introns are cut out of the newly made RNA, and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus." She pointed at her timeline. "The introns are my bad takes. The goose, the dog, the ums. The exons are the parts I keep. And the finished video, the spliced version, is what actually goes out. The edited message is the one that leaves."

Kasey leaned over the laptop. "So the nucleus is like the editing room," Kasey said slowly. "The raw footage never goes anywhere. Only the cut version does."

"Before it leaves," Alexia said, tapping the word on her screen. "That's the part I kept skipping. The splicing happens before it leaves the nucleus. It's not optional. It's not cleanup that happens later, somewhere else. If it doesn't get cut and spliced first, the messenger RNA doesn't go out at all." She thought of all the times she had sent a text too fast and regretted it, though that was a small comparison and she let it go.

Noelle had stopped reading her textbook and was watching the geese drift near the reeds. "I still don't get why cells would make the extra stuff in the first place," she said. "Why copy the bad takes at all if they're just going to be cut?"

Alexia had no answer for that. She looked at her own timeline, where the goose honk still sat in her trash folder, recoverable if she wanted it. Maybe the cell had its reasons and the chapter had not told them yet, or maybe the reasons were the kind that only showed up later, in some chapter she would not read until college. She was honest enough with herself to sit with that instead of inventing something. "I don't know," she said. "That part's still open. But for tomorrow, I can walk through the whole thing in order, and I can say exactly what gets cut and what gets spliced and when. That might be enough."

"It has to be," Kasey said. "Test's at nine."

They stayed until the light went amber over the water. Noelle made them each recite the sequence twice, then a third time with eyes closed, and Kasey kept calling the introns "the goose parts" until it stuck so thoroughly that they were both laughing. Alexia exported her finished documentary and watched the full version once, end to end, all the bad takes gone and the good pieces joined so cleanly that no one watching would ever guess what had been removed.

At the path's turn she stopped and looked back at the pond, at the reeds and the darkening water and the bench still holding their shape in the grass. Then she picked up her bag, caught up with Kasey, and said, "Ask me again. From the top. Nuclear membrane, and go."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
story:
The current map covered most of the lab table, and Cole had been staring at it long enough that the red arrows had started to look like veins. Ms. Ferreira had taped it down herself at the start of the period, then said only, "Presentation tomorrow. I want one of you to be able to explain to a stranger why northern Europe is warmer than it has any right to be." Then she had gone to her desk to grade quizzes, which was her way of saying the map was the teacher now.

Cole wanted the presentation. He had scored lowest in the class on the first quiz, a 61 that Theresa had seen when the papers were passed back, and she hadn't said anything, which was somehow worse. So he had stayed after the bell, and Kiefer had stayed because Kiefer never went home when there was anything to avoid doing, and Theresa had stayed because, she said, her house was loud.

"There," Kiefer said, tapping the North Atlantic. "What even is that." The arrows swept northeast off the American coast, crossed the ocean in a wide red river, and broke against the coasts of Ireland and Norway. Cole traced them with one finger, the way Ms. Ferreira had shown them, careful not to smudge the laminated surface. "That's the Gulf Stream," he said. "Warm water moving north. It heats the air above it, the wind carries the air east, Europe gets warm." It sounded good. It sounded like the textbook. He said it again, more slowly, to make sure.

"So then why is Norway warm but Newfoundland is cold?" Theresa asked. She had pulled a chair up backwards and was resting her chin on its back. "They're about the same latitude. That's the question she asked us last week."

Cole opened his mouth to answer and found nothing there. He looked at the map again, following the red river farther and farther north, past Iceland, past the top of Scandinavia, until the arrows thinned into a thread that curved around Norway's cap and kept going, into the gray space near the top of the sheet where the ink got faint.

"Wait," he said. "Where does that go?"

"Russia," Theresa said. "That little label there. Murmansk."

Cole leaned in. Murmansk sat north of the line the map printed as a dashed circle, and below the name, in small type, the map's key read: ice-free year-round. He read it three times. "That's inside the Arctic Circle," he said. "Above it. Whatever. That's above the Arctic Circle, and it's ice-free all year. In winter. Ships can get in and out all winter."

"Because of the warm water," Kiefer said slowly, following the same thread with his eyes. "The current carries it all the way there." He sounded like he didn't believe himself, which Cole respected, because he didn't believe it either, and because it was true anyway. The water that left the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf Stream became something else by the time it reached those latitudes, the North Atlantic Current, and it was that water, the map insisted, that kept a Russian port above the Arctic Circle open in January.

"So my answer was wrong," Cole said. "Not wrong. Half right. It's not the Gulf Stream that warms Europe, not by the time it gets there. It's what the Gulf Stream turns into." He thought of his 61, and of how he had written a whole paragraph about winds and latitude and gotten the one real mechanism only halfway. The ocean sequestered its heat in motion, carrying it for thousands of miles, releasing it somewhere no one would expect. It was like learning that the school's heat came from a boiler in a building across town.

Theresa had gone quiet in a way that Cole had learned to watch for. "My bio homework is going to be a disaster," she said finally. "I've been reading about antigens for an hour and I still couldn't tell you what one is." She was looking at the map, though, not at her phone.

"Explain it to us tomorrow," Cole said. "Like a stranger. That's what she wants." He tapped Murmansk. "Start here. A port above the Arctic Circle that never freezes. Nobody believes it, and then you show them the water." He began rolling the map, and Kiefer held the far edge flat so it wouldn't crease.

"Wait, who's presenting?" Kiefer asked. "You said you wanted it."

Cole looked at Theresa, who was still frowning at the spot where Murmansk had been, as if the ink might reveal something more. "All three of us," she said. "You do the current, I'll do the bio part later, and Kiefer can point at things."

Kiefer pointed at the map, which was now a cylinder, and then at Cole, and then at the clock. "Dinner's in twenty minutes," he said. "Walk fast."

Ms. Ferreira looked up from her quizzes as they gathered their bags, and Cole held up the rolled map so she could see it. "Murmansk," he said. She raised one eyebrow and went back to grading.

Outside, the October wind came off the school's riparian side, where the path ran along the creek, and it was warm for the season, and Cole caught himself wondering where that wind had been before it got here.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
The flyer went up on a Tuesday: the regional econ showcase, presentations on Friday, sign-ups closing Wednesday at noon. Maika wrote her name in the third slot before she could talk herself out of it, and only afterward did she admit to herself what she had signed up to explain: why a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had a textbook chapter, a half-page of notes, and the sinking sense that she was reciting rather than understanding.

"Nobody in that room wants a lecture," Marilie said at lunch, poking at her rice. "Mr. Yip will sit in the back row and grade you on whether a normal person could follow it."

"I don't follow it myself yet."

"Then you have two days. That's practically luxurious."

It was not luxurious. Wednesday evening Maika sat at the library table with the chapter open to the same paragraph she'd read four times, about aggregate demand and monetary transmission, and each pass the words slid off her like water off glass. She understood biology this way once, too, before she'd sorted organisms into phylum after phylum and found that the categories held. Economics refused to hold still. The graphs balanced on arrows pointing at other arrows, and every explanation seemed to rest on something further back that no one had told her.

Then Ali dropped into the chair across from her, still in his apron from the coffee shop, and slid his phone across the table. "Tell me if I'm being stupid," he said. The screen showed his bank app. His savings account rate had gone up. "I was going to buy the new phone Friday, payday. Now the account's paying more, and I'm sitting here doing math on napkins like a lunatic. Is saving it actually the better move?"

Maika looked at the number, then at her notes, and felt something click into place with an almost audible sensation. "Wait. That's it. That's the whole thing." She pulled the chapter toward her. "When rates go up, the bank pays you more to keep money there. So you save instead of buying. And if everyone's a little bit you, then people are spending less on stuff overall."

"So the phone loses."

"So demand for the phone drops. And when there's less buying happening, prices stop climbing so fast." She said it out loud twice more, differently each time, testing it. Higher rates paid savers more, so households shifted money from spending into savings, which lowered demand for goods and helped slow price rises. It fit in a sentence. It fit in a napkin doodle, which she drew while Ali watched: a stick figure with a phone in one hand and a piggy bank in the other, the piggy bank getting heavier.

Ali bought her a terrible vending-machine coffee as payment and took his napkin with him. He said he'd sleep on the phone. Marilie, when Maika explained it to her by phone that night, was quiet for a moment and then said, "You know, I was going to skip the showcase. I figured I'd present the tariffs thing and tank it. But if you can build it like that, off one real decision a person makes, maybe I'll do mine after all. Mine's on rent control and I've been burying it in jargon because I thought that's what sounded smart."

"That is the opposite of smart," Maika said. "I have forty minutes of a textbook chapter proving it."

Friday morning the showcase room smelled of floor wax and nerves. Mr. Yip sat in the back with a clipboard and the expression of a man who had heard a hundred recitations of the transmission mechanism and survived them all. Maika had considered drafting trenchant opening lines, something to announce her competence, but she'd cut them, and she was glad, because when her turn came she began instead with Ali and his apron and his phone.

"Friday's payday," she told the room. "One of you might be deciding tonight between a new phone and a savings account. Here's what the central bank did to that decision." She held up the napkin, because it was honest, and walked them through it: the higher rate pays savers more, so some money that would have been spent gets saved instead, demand for goods falls, and rising prices start to slow. A girl in the second row raised her hand and asked what happened if everyone saved and nobody bought anything. Maika said that was a real question and that she didn't fully know the answer, but that she suspected the central bank was watching the same thing and could turn the rate back down. Mr. Yip wrote something on his clipboard without looking up.

Afterward Ali was waiting by the door, hands in his pockets. "So I decided," he said. "Savings account. Phone in the spring, maybe, if it still matters." He shrugged, a little sheepish. "It felt weird, like the responsible adult version of me absconded with my paycheck. But the number's going up instead of down." He tapped his phone against his palm, then slid it into his back pocket, unspent.

Marilie's name was called from inside the room. She stood, squared her shoulders, and walked in carrying a stack of index cards that she promptly turned face-down on the podium.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
The bell above the bookshop door had a habit of sticking in warm weather, so Sophie gave it a thump on her way in, the way Ms. Esposito liked, and the smell of dust and old glue greeted her like a cat that pretended not to care. In the back, under the shelf of yellowed Dickens paperbacks, three folding chairs were already taken. Ely sat with an enormous cookie balanced on a paperback's spine. Walker had his copy of Pride and Prejudice open but was reading something else entirely inside it, which Sophie knew because it had no cover.

"Who's presenting?" Walker asked, mouth full.

"I am," Sophie said, and immediately regretted the confidence, because presenting meant she had to have a position, and she had spent the whole week with two positions glowering at each other across her notes like siblings in the back seat of a car.

Ms. Esposito poured tea from a thermos that had survived, by her own account, three decades of book clubs and one house fire. "Take your time, Sophie. The till won't ring until six."

Sophie flipped to the page she'd flagged, the passage where Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth, oily and unbothered, and read aloud until Ely started laughing at the phrase "violence of my affection." "He means it as a compliment," Ely said. "That's the best part. He means everything as a compliment."
