"Here's my Marxist reading," Sophie began, and laid it out: the Bennets are gentry but the gentry runs on money like everyone else, marriage is a market, Mr Collins is a man whose entire value is his inheritance, and Elizabeth is being asked to trade herself into it. "So the proposal scene is basically a transaction where nobody says the price out loud."

"And your feminist reading?" Ms. Esposito asked, in the tone of someone who already suspected the answer.

"That's the problem," Sophie admitted. "Because the feminist reading keeps colliding with it. Like Mrs Bennet. My first draft had her down as a hysterical embarrassment, which is how the narrator plays her. But then I found the thing about the estate." She checked her notes. "The whole estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home. The house itself. They can't have it. If Mr Bennet dies, Collins gets it and the daughters are out."

There was a small silence, the kind where a room rearranges its opinion.

"Wait," Walker said, sitting up, the hidden book sliding shut. "So Mrs Bennet's matchmaking, the panic, the husband-hunting, all of it. It's not madness. It's arithmetic."

"It sort of exonerates her," Sophie said. "Or at least it convicts her of something smaller than I charged her with. I called her a hedonist obsessed with marrying off her daughters for sport, and that's unfair. She's not in it for pleasure. The pleasure is fake. The fear is real."

Ely licked a crumb off her thumb. "So the Marxist lens says the whole family is trapped in a money machine, and the feminist lens says the trap has a lock only the daughters can feel. And they're both right and they're arguing anyway."

"They're both right and they point in the same direction, most of the time," Sophie said. "Which is what I didn't expect. I thought I'd have to pick. Like the lenses were parsimonious with the truth, each one hoarding its own piece. But Mrs Bennet makes the most sense standing in both at once." She hesitated, then said the part she'd rehearsed least. "What I still can't decide is Elizabeth. Refusing Collins is brave and it's principled and it's also a bet she can afford because Jane is pretty and she is clever. I don't know what the lenses say about luck. Neither one has a chapter on luck."

Ms. Esposito smiled into her tea. "Some questions stay open longer than the book does. That's not a failure of the reading, that's the reading."

"That's a very convenient thing for a teacher to say," Walker said, and everyone laughed, and Ms. Esposito didn't argue, which Sophie took as evidence in his favor.

Ely raised the cookie like a gavel. "Motion to exonerate Mrs Bennet of all charges except volume."

"Seconded, with an asterisk," Sophie said. "The asterisk is Wickham. Nobody's exonerated of Wickham."

Walker leaned across and tapped her notebook. "So what's your considered position? You have to write one. It's due Tuesday."

Sophie looked at the two columns of her notes, the market and the marriage, the money and the daughters, and then at the sticky note she'd left herself at the bottom that said only, luck?? She closed the notebook, and out front the bell finally unstuck itself and rang for a customer nobody had thumped.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The bread sat on the cutting board like a argument Nicolas had lost. He pressed a finger into the crumb and it crumbled, dense and dry, a brick with ambitions of being a loaf. His mother had eaten two slices anyway, quietly, with butter, which somehow made it worse.

He had made it because she came home from the hospital shift with that grey malaise she carried now, the one that settled over the kitchen and made everyone speak in half sentences. His father had left a note about a late meeting. Nicolas had found the recipe in his grandmother's handwriting, flour still ghosted in the creases, and decided that a warm loaf would fix something, though he couldn't have said what.

Saturday morning he took the bus to the grocery store with his mother's list and his own plan folded in his pocket. He stood too long in the baking aisle, holding a bag of bread flour in each hand as though they might confess their differences. Kathryn found him there, stacking items into a handbasket with the brisk efficiency of someone on an errand timer.

"You're the one who brought the brick to Sam's thing," she said. "Sam called it artisanal. He was being polite."

"It was underproofed. Or over. Or something." He put one bag back. "It was bad."

"Maybe you needed different flour. That's a thing, right? Protein, or whatever."

He shrugged, blasé in a way he didn't feel, because admitting he cared would mean admitting how much. "Could be anything."

They drifted toward the checkout together. At the register, Ms. Augustin from his chemistry class was bagging her own groceries, and she raised an eyebrow at his single bag of flour, the yeast, the jar of honey.

"Second attempt?" she said.

"How did you know?"

"Nobody buys yeast for the first attempt until after the funeral." She smiled, then grew serious. "My mother baked every Sunday for forty years. She used to say you could tell a loaf by its hands."

Nicolas didn't ask what that meant. He paid and carried the bag out into the cold.

At home he cleared the counter and turned on the radio for company. The first loaf had gone wrong somewhere, and he needed to find the fork in the road where he'd taken the bad path. He measured the flour the way the recipe said. He added the water, watched it darken the white powder into shaggy clumps, and then he turned the mass out and began to press and fold.

Twenty minutes of kneading, the recipe had said, or until smooth and elastic. He had gone maybe ten, last time, arms aching, bored, certain it was enough. Now he worked the dough longer, and something changed under his hands. The surface went from ragged to silky. When he stretched a piece, it thinned into a window instead of tearing, a translucent film he could see the radio light through.

He was still turning it over, thinking about that window, when Sam texted: did the brick have a sequel. Nicolas typed back, not yet, and kept kneading. His arms burned. He kept going.

The second rise worked better too, the dough climbing the bowl's rim like it had somewhere to be. He shaped it, slashed the top with a razor because Kathryn had told him bakers did that, and slid it into the oven on the preheated sheet. Then he sat on the kitchen floor with the recipe and his phone, looking up what he had actually done, because it didn't seem fair that aching arms should matter more than careful measuring.

He found it in a baking forum, an argument between two strangers that went on for forty posts. The proteins in wheat flour, one of them wrote, glutenin and gliadin, don't become gluten until they meet water. And kneading, the other one added before the thread dissolved into insults, builds the network; kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger, and the bread chewier. Nicolas read it twice. So the first loaf hadn't been bad flour or bad yeast. It had been ten minutes of kneading where twenty were needed, a network left half-built, unable to hold the air the yeast made. The crumb had collapsed because nothing was holding it up.

He texted Sam: it was the kneading. Sam replied with a thumbs up and the word nerd.

When the loaf came out, it sang. He'd read about that, the crackling sound bread makes as it cools, and had assumed it was a myth, but there it was, a faint ticking from the crust as it shrank against the crumb. He tapped the bottom and it sounded hollow, which the recipe promised meant done. He waited, because the recipe said to wait, and the waiting was the hardest part.

His mother came home while it was still too hot to cut. She stood in the doorway with her coat on, keys in her hand, and looked at the loaf on the rack, then at the flour dusted across his forearms and one eyebrow.

"You baked," she said.

"Attempt two."

"And the first one?"

"Sam's calling it artisanal."

She laughed, a real one, and hung up her coat. She got the bread knife from the drawer and handed it to him, handle first, and stood beside him at the board while he set the blade against the crust. The knife went through with resistance and then with none, and the slice fell away showing a crumb full of holes, open and ragged and alive, nothing like the brick. She took a piece before he'd finished cutting, tore off a corner, and ate it standing up.

"Chewy," she said, reaching for another slice.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Connecting words such as Spanish 'sin embargo', meaning 'however', let a debater signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of their grammar is simple.
story:
The library had a back corner where the geography atlases went unread, and Zoe had claimed it for weeks now, spreading her Spanish notes across two tables like a lawyer preparing a case she could not yet argue. In five days, Mr. Nakamura's Spanish seminar would hold its first full debate, and every student had to speak for five minutes, entirely in Spanish, on whether the school should switch to a later start time. Five minutes. Zoe could barely manage thirty seconds before her sentences collapsed into a list of nouns with verbs dangling off them like loose threads.

She had tried again that afternoon, phone timer balanced against a globe of the Andes. The school is tired. Students need sleep. Sleep helps the brain. The brain is important. She had stopped the timer at forty seconds and put her forehead on the table.

"You sound like a fortune cookie," said Audrina, dropping into the chair across from her with her own stack of flashcards. Audrina wanted the debate to go well for a different reason: she was applying to a summer program that required a language teacher's recommendation, and Mr. Nakamura had told the class that the strongest debater would be noticed. Zoe knew this, and Audrina knew she knew, and neither of them said it, which was its own kind of vocabulary lesson.

"My grammar is fine," Zoe said. "It's just..." She waved at her notes. "It's all these separate boxes. First this. Then this. Then this."

Scarlet arrived late, obstreperous as always, her backpack clattering against the atlas shelf before she even reached the table. She had spent a semester in Cuenca and spoke with an ease that made the other two quiet. "What are you fighting about?" she asked, stealing Audrina's crackers.

"Nothing. That's the problem." Zoe slid her notes across. "Read it and tell me what's broken."

Scarlet read. Her mouth did something between a wince and a laugh. "You're not arguing. You're just stating things in a row. In Spanish you need the connectors or nobody hears a counterargument. You know 'sin embargo'?"

Zoe shook her head.

"It means 'however.' You put it in and suddenly the sentence on the other side has to be answered." Scarlet tapped the page. "It works even if your grammar is simple. The listener hears the turn."

Zoe sat back and let herself cogitate on this for a moment, turning the phrase over the way she turned a proof in geometry, testing whether it held. Her sentences did not need to be more complicated. They needed hinges. Por una parte, the school is tired. Sin embargo, the bus schedule is expensive. Suddenly her notes were not boxes in a row but two voices, and she was the one deciding which one to trust, which was not something she had expected from a language exercise.

She built the whole argument again on a clean page. Students need sleep; sin embargo, a later start means later sports practice in the dark; the brain is important; sin embargo, so is the bus budget. She was not an ideologue on this issue, she realized, and the connectors let her say so without surrendering either side. She read it aloud, quietly, and even Audrina stopped shuffling flashcards.

Then Mr. Nakamura himself came around the atlas shelf with a book on hold, and Zoe covered her page with her arm before she could think about why. He raised an eyebrow. "Practicing for Friday?"

"Yes," Audrina said quickly, and something in her voice made Zoe look up. Audrina had her flashcards fanned out, and Zoe understood, in one uncomfortable second, that Audrina had been sitting here listening to every draft, that Audrina had heard the forty seconds of fortune cookies, that Audrina knew exactly how far behind Zoe had been and might still be.

"Good," Mr. Nakamura said. "I'll tell you now, since you're all here. Friday, you won't argue the side you prepared. You'll draw it from a hat."

He walked away with his book. Scarlet broke the silence first, whistling low. "So all your hinges," she said, pointing at Zoe's covered page, "they'll be turning the wrong way."

Zoe looked down at the page under her arm. Por una parte. Sin embargo. If she drew the other side, every however would have to point somewhere new, and she was not sure yet whether that made the words useless or whether it made them the only part of her argument she could carry across the line intact. Across the table, Audrina was already writing, not looking up.

"Audrina," Zoe said. "When did you figure out the connectors?"

Audrina kept her pen moving. "Last week."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The community field had been mowed into stripes for the occasion, and someone had hung a bedsheet between the goalposts so the projector would have something to shine on. By the time the Olympic final started, half the neighborhood was folded into folding chairs, and Sierra sat cross-legged on the grass between her father and Yan, a paper plate of ribs cooling in her lap. On the sheet, before the match, the broadcast kept returning to an animated version of the rings, five circles tumbling and locking together while a voice talked about unity.

"There," Sierra said, pointing with a rib. "Watch the rings. I read about them last night."

"You read about circles," Yan said. The game hadn't started yet and he was bored enough to be cruel about it.

"Pierre de Coubertin designed them in 1913," she said. "He picked the colors so that every national flag at the time contained at least one of them. Including the white background. So nobody was left out." She said it carefully, the way she had rehearsed it walking over, because she had decided it mattered and wanted to get it right.

Her father leaned back on his palms. He had played semi-pro somewhere, years ago, and he watched even commercials with the patient stillness of a man waiting for a whistle. "Colors on a flag never fed anybody," he said. "You want to belong to something, belong to a team. That's the only symbol that counts." It sounded like an aphorism he had polished over years, the kind he produced at dinner tables and in car rides, and usually she absorbed these without argument.

But Eugenie, sprawled on the other side of Yan with her sandals off, sat up. "That's not true though. Symbols do work. My mom cried at a flag once." She said it defiantly, daring anyone to laugh. Nobody did. The whistle blew on the sheet and the field went loud, parents shouting advice to players who could not hear them, and for twenty minutes the argument dissolved into the game itself.

Sierra found she was not really watching the match. She was watching the crowd around her, the way Eugenie's whole body angled toward the screen whenever their country touched the ball, the way her father's shoulders dropped when the other side scored first. She turned both positions over the way she turned a coin. Her father wanted belonging to be earned, physical, something you sweated for; Eugenie wanted it to be given, woven into the fabric before you arrived. Sierra had always assumed she had to choose between them, the way you chose a side of a field. But the rings themselves seemed to say otherwise. Someone had sat down, in 1913, and made a design decision that nobody would ever notice on purpose, so that no flag in the world would look at the symbol and find itself absent. That was sweat and fabric both. An engineer's version of welcome.

She tried to say some of this to Yan during halftime, and it came out tangled. "It's like, the inclusion was designed in, before anyone felt included. So maybe the feeling and the design aren't opposites. Maybe the feeling gets built." She knew she was being tangential, that Yan wanted to talk about the defense, that a boy two rows back was already shouting for a substitution. "But I can't actually prove the design caused the feeling. That part I don't know."

"That part you don't know," Yan agreed, mouth full of chips. He was kind enough not to problematize it further, which was his way of being a friend.

The second half was cruel. Their team equalized in the seventieth minute, and the field erupted, and Eugenie grabbed Sierra's arm hard enough to leave marks, and the game went to extra time, and then, in the last minute of it, a defender slipped on the wet grass and the ball went in at the far post. Nobody spoke. On the sheet, the players in the wrong-colored shirts ran toward their corner of the world, and the commentary said something gracious that no one heard. Eugenie lay back flat in the grass and stared at the sky.

Sierra's father gathered the plates without a word. That was his symbol, Sierra thought, watching him stack them into a neat white tower: work, done quietly, at the end of things. The broadcast cut back to the rings one last time, blue, yellow, black, green, red, floating on the white of the bedsheet, and she understood, suddenly and completely, that she and Eugenie had spent the whole match looking for their country inside those five circles, and finding it, and being wrong and right at the same time.

Eugenie sat up, followed her gaze to the sheet, and started to laugh, a raw, surprised sound.

"Ours is the background," she said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
The farmers' market opened at eight, and by quarter past Brayden was standing at the onion bin with a paper sack half full, counting coins in his head. His mother had left a note on the counter before her shift, the same note as every Friday: soup, whatever looks good, don't let the milk spoil. His father's absence had settled over the kitchen like weather, and after three months of it, Brayden had stopped waiting for the note to change and started acceding to the fact that dinner was his now.

"You're the one who made that soup at the potluck," Karma said, appearing beside him with her own bag, empty and ambitious. "The one everybody talked about." She worked Saturdays at the market for Mr. Lawson, hauling baskets and making change, and she was saving for a culinary intensive in the city, a summer program she'd mentioned so often the price had become a kind of refrain. "What's in it this time?"

"Onions, mostly. Leeks if they're cheap. Potatoes, garlic." He weighed the bag in his palm. "Everything worth eating starts with an onion."

"Then buy mine," said Ahmed, who was stacking crates behind his father's table at the end of the row, under a canvas awning that snapped whenever the wind came off the river. Ahmed's father grew shallots and onions on a small plot outside town, and Ahmed had been arguing all morning that the vegetables deserved shade, not sun, a disagreement conducted entirely through the placement of crates. "These are better than the supermarket ones. Cut one and you'll see."

"You'll cry, you mean," Karma said.

Brayden paid for the onions and the leeks, argued the price of potatoes down by a quarter, and walked back through the stalls with the sack against his hip. Mr. Lawson was at his table arranging jars of honey, and when Brayden stopped to say good morning, the old man only nodded toward Karma, who was counting her till with the concentration of someone who knew exactly what the number needed to be and how far short it fell. "Tell her the intensive takes my niece's kids half the summer," Mr. Lawson said. "She'll figure the rest out herself."

At home, Brayden spread the vegetables across the counter and found his sister already at the table, eleven years old and pretending to do homework. He set the cutting board down, took the largest onion, and halved it, then quartered it, then began the slow work of the dice. Within a minute his sister had pushed her chair back from the table and pressed her sleeve against her eyes.

"It's the smell," she said, muffled.

"It's not the smell." He kept cutting. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce a vapor, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, and it irritates your eyes. That's all it is." He wiped his own cheek with his shoulder. "It gets me too. Everyone."

"Then why do you keep doing it?"

Because the soup needed it. Because the note on the counter was the only thing his mother asked of him and he intended to get it right. He didn't say any of that. He said, "Because it's good," and slid the onions into the pot with the oil already shimmering, and the kitchen filled with the sound of them softening.

His sister came back to the table, red-eyed and interested despite herself, and watched him work through the leeks and the garlic. He let her peel the garlic because she asked, and she sat with the papery skins in a heap and said, "Karma's here," nodding at the window. Karma stood on the porch with a sack of her own, and when Brayden opened the door she held it out. "Shallots," she said. "From Ahmed. He said to tell you they're from the shaded crates, so if they're terrible, it proves his father right and he loses the argument."

"Come in. There's soup in an hour."

She came in and stood in the kitchen with her coat still on, watching him stir. "Mr. Lawson told you," she said. It wasn't a question. She set the shallots on the counter. "About the money. That it's not going to happen this summer."

"He said his niece's kids take half the summer. That's all."

"Then you inferred the rest." She pulled out a chair at the table, across from his sister, and started helping with the garlic skins, brushing them into her palm. "I've got two hundred saved. I need nine hundred. At the rate I'm going, it's attrition. I'll get there the summer after, and by then everyone who went this year will be ahead of me."

Brayden tasted the broth and added salt. He had been thinking, without quite letting himself think it, about the difference between his mother's note and Karma's nine hundred dollars, between the things asked of you and the things you asked of yourself. His father had wanted something else, evidently, something that a kitchen and a Friday soup couldn't supply, and his mother had acceded to that too, in her way, by leaving notes instead of questions. Maybe that was weakness and maybe it was just arithmetic, the slow counting of what was possible. He didn't know. He knew the onions were sweating down properly and the potatoes needed cutting.

"Chop those," he said, sliding the sack toward her.

Karma took the paring knife and a potato and worked in silence for a while, his sister watching her technique with open admiration. When Karma had finished the potatoes she reached, almost absently, for one of Ahmed's shallots, peeled it, and began to mince it fine. A minute later her eyes were streaming. Brayden's sister pointed and laughed, delighted, and Karma laughed too, wiping her face with the heel of her hand, and said, "It's not crying, it's chemistry," and kept mincing.

Outside, the light was going amber over the rooftops, and the maples along the street had gone fully arboreal in the last warm week, their shade lying across the porch in long stripes. Brayden opened the window over the sink to let the steam out, and the three of them worked in the small kitchen until the soup was thick and the bowls were on the table, and Karma, holding hers with both hands, said, "Next year, then. You'll teach me the soup and I'll teach you the knife work."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
The gallery was cold in the way that suggested art preferred people to be slightly uncomfortable, and Alice had been standing in front of the same photograph for eleven minutes. It showed a woman in a blonde wig, leaning against a kitchen doorway, looking off to the side as though someone just off camera had said something she intended to ignore. Beside her, Sahana was reading the wall text out loud in the voice she used for mocking museum solemnity, a kind of breathy documentary narrator.

"Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills," Sahana read, "1977 to 1980." She squinted at the small print. "Seventy photographs. All of them are her. She poses as characters from movies that don't exist."

"Seventy," Alice said. The number sat in her chest like a stone dropped into a pond, rings spreading outward. Seventy images of one face, and none of them the same woman.

"That's deranged," said Makayla, arriving with three postcards from the gift shop fanned out in her hand like a losing poker hand. "Imagine doing your face seventy times."

"Imagine doing it ten times," Alice said, and then, because she had been carrying the problem around for two weeks like a pebble in her shoe, she told them. The portfolio. Ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement by December. She had chosen self-portraits, because she was free that way, cheap and always available, and now every sketch she made looked like the same girl in the same hoodie with the same worried eyebrows. "It's a quagmire," she said. "Every time I try to fix it I sink deeper. Yesterday I drew myself as a vampire to mix it up and it just looked like me with bad teeth."

"Vampires are cool though," Makayla said, holding up a postcard. "This one's the blonde one. Two dollars. Cheaper than the book."

Ms. Sokolov, who had been drifting through the room with her coat over her arm like a woman who had opinions about every frame, came to stand beside them. "You've found the Film Stills," she said. "When I was your age I tried to copy the hotel one with a towel on my head and my mother's sunglasses. The exposure was wrong and I looked like a burglar."

Alice laughed, and Sahana said, "Send it to us," and Ms. Sokolov said she would not, and they walked on into the next room, where the photographs continued along the wall, one after another, women in offices, women on roads, women staring into mirrors with expressions that belonged to noir films no one had ever made.

Alice walked slowly and let them get ahead. The hallway of strangers who were all one person did something to her thinking that she could not have described if asked, the way a key does something to a lock without your seeing the mechanism. Each photograph was posed like a still from a scene, and the scene was missing on purpose. The woman on the road was running from something. The woman at the mirror was deciding something. The pictures told you there had been a movie, and the movie was your invention. Seventy of them, and each one a different imaginary film, and the connective tissue was not the face but the premise.

She caught up with the others at the bench near the window. "Okay," she said. "I think I had the theme backwards. I kept trying to make ten portraits of me, and the problem is me. I'm impervious to my own imagination. I look at my face and I just see Tuesday."

"Impervious," Makayla repeated, delighted. "You've been studying the word list."

"Some of them stuck. But look." Alice flipped open her sketchbook to the page where she had been doodling during the train ride, a drawing of herself as a museum guard, as a flight attendant, as a girl being told devastating news over the phone. "What if the theme isn't me. It's me as characters from stories that don't exist. Each one is a still from a movie nobody made, and the statement is about how a person is partly made of the roles she's never played."

Sahana leaned over the doodles. "The flight attendant one has your exact eyebrows. The worried ones."

"Fine, she's a flight attendant with anxiety about turbulence. Some things are constants." Alice was speaking faster now, pencil moving. "Ten pieces, ten fake films, and the wall label for each one gives the invented title. Like Untitled Film Still number whatever, except mine would have titles because I'm not trying to be cool about it."

"It's stealing," Makayla said, but she said it the way you say it when you mostly mean it's good.

"It's borrowing a structure," Alice said. "Sherman borrowed the structure from movies. I'm borrowing it from her. That's how structures work, they enfranchise the next person, they don't get used up." She paused. "Although I should probably say in the statement that the series is influenced by her, or Ms. Sokolov will write 'derivative?' in the margin like she did with my Cornell boxes."

"I wrote 'derivative?' once," Ms. Sokolov said from behind them, because of course she was there, "and it was about your glue choices."

At the window, the light had gone the flat grey of late afternoon, and Alice sat with the sketchbook on her knees, not drawing yet, turning over the one thing that still bothered her. Sherman had made seventy, over three years, becoming an entire population of women who had never existed. Ten felt suddenly small, almost timid, and yet she knew herself well enough to know that ten was what she could actually carry through a winter of school. Maybe the honest version of the theme included that limit. Maybe her statement could admit that she was one girl with a part-time job and a bus pass, not a studio and a decade. She didn't know yet. She wrote a question mark next to the flight attendant and underlined it twice.

"Earth to Alice," Sahana said. "They're closing the side rooms in ten minutes."

"Then I need to see the mirror one again before they lock it." Alice stood, tucked the pencil behind her ear, and set off back down the hallway at a pace just short of running, past the blonde in the doorway who was still ignoring whoever was off camera, heading for the woman at the mirror who had never once looked at her own reflection.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
The worksheet arrived on Friday, due Monday, and William had carried it in his backpack through the whole weekend without opening it. Now it was Sunday afternoon, and he sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with the paper finally unfolded in front of him: a population pyramid for Japan, bars fanning out in five-year bands, males on the left, females on the right. Mr. Sultani had assigned it with a single question at the bottom. Would this country need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years, and how could you tell?

The house smelled like his grandfather's coffee, strong enough to suture the afternoon together. His grandfather was at the counter slicing a pear, unhurried, and William was grateful for that, because the worksheet had already defeated him twice at home. He had texted Krish a photo of the pyramid and gotten back a shrug of an emoji and the message "no clue man, the left side is boys right?" which was technically an answer and entirely useless.

"Is that for Mr. Sultani?" his grandfather asked, setting a plate of pear slices beside the paper.

"Geography. We have to say whether they'll build more schools or more nursing homes." William slid the sheet across. "The bottom's wide, the middle's narrow, the top's small. I think."

His grandfather put on his glasses and bent over the page. William watched him, half embarrassed, as if he were being tutored by a man who confused the remote controls. But the old man traced a finger up the right side of the pyramid and paused near the top.

"Why is it lopsided up here?" his grandfather asked. "On your graph, I mean. The women's side sticks out farther than the men's, right at the top."

William leaned in. He had not noticed it. All the way up the chart, band after band, the female bars on the right ran slightly longer than the male bars on the left, and the difference grew toward the top, until in the oldest band the right side reached out almost twice as far. "Huh," he said. "Maybe they count more old women. Maybe the data's wrong."

"Or women live longer than men," his grandfather said, and returned to his pear, as though he had remarked on the weather.

William turned this over while chewing a slice. If the top of most pyramids has more women than men because women live longer than men on average, then the chart was not lopsided by accident; it was lopsided everywhere, in every country, a quiet bias built into the shape itself. He thought of his grandmother, gone four years now, and his grandfather still here, and how in his own family the fact had run the other way, and he set that thought down carefully, like a plate he did not want to break.

He worked through the rest with the pencil his grandfather lent him, the eraser chewed flat. The bottom bands of Japan's pyramid were pinched, narrower than his own age group would be in Canada; the middle bulged where the big cohorts sat, and above them the pyramid widened again in relative terms as the bars thinned. More nursing homes, he wrote, because the population was aging, and the narrowing base meant fewer children to fill schools. Then he stopped. He was a pragmatist about most things, happy to take the answer that worked, but he had learned in Mr. Sultani's class that a single chart could not carry the whole truth. Immigration could widen the base. Nursing homes could become something else by then. He wrote a second paragraph admitting all of it, and the admission felt less like weakness than like honesty.

On Monday he found Lacey in the hallway before third period, comparing answers with Krish. "I put nursing homes," Krish said. "All the old people. Lacey said schools, because of the bottom, but the bottom's tiny."

"That's why it's nursing homes," Lacey conceded, reading William's page. Then she tapped the top of the chart. "What's this about, though? Your note here, about the women's side being wider."

William looked at her over Krish's shoulder. "That's the part my grandfather caught. I missed it twice."

He showed them, running his pencil up the right edge, the three of them bent close in the crowded hallway while the warning bell rang and nobody moved yet.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Eric had been volunteered into coaching before he quite understood what coaching was. Mr. Castillo, who ran the winter skills clinic for the under-twelves at the rink beside the track, had cornered him after Eric's own practice one Tuesday, holding a clipboard full of notes and the expression of a man distributing blame. "Your passing drills," Mr. Castillo said, tapping the clipboard, "are on you now. The whole page. Read it tonight." The whole page said, in Mr. Castillo's cramped capitals, PASSING DELETERIOUS. OPPOSING STICKS. FIX. Eric had looked up deleterious on the bus home, because Mr. Castillo was the sort of man who used words like that and expected you to keep up.

The problem was easy to see and hard to fix. Every pass the kids made traveled along the ice, and every pass died on the blade of some small, gleeful defender. Eric had watched two games' worth of it from the bench, cold coffee in his mitt, doing the arithmetic of despair. Six blocked passes in the first period alone. The kids were not bad; they were just predictable, and predictable at ankle height.

The rink shared its parking lot with the running track, and Eric did some of his best thinking while walking the oval's cracked third lane, which was why Christopher found him there Thursday after school, lap four of an aimless circuit. "You look like a detective in a bad show," Christopher said, falling into step. "Walk and deduce." "I'm designing drills," Eric said. "Mr. Castillo gave me a page. It says deleterious on it." "Sounds fatal." "Everything's fatal to him."

What Eric had worked out, halfway through lap three, was that he was thinking about the problem from the wrong side. He had been trying to make the passes faster, so the sticks would miss. But the sticks were small and slow, and the passes were slow too, and speed was a race the weakest hands on the team would lose. Better, he thought, to go over. Height. Lift the puck, let it travel in the air, come down on the tape. He said as much to Christopher, who squinted at the November sky as if the sky might contradict him. "Can twelve-year-olds even do that?" "I don't know," Eric said. "That's the experiment."

Luis, the smallest and loudest of the under-twelves, was against the whole idea on principle. Luis wanted one thing from the clinic, which was to be made captain, and captains, in Luis's cosmology, scored goals; they did not spend an hour learning to flip a puck like a pancake. "This is goalie practice," Luis announced, when Eric set out the cones on Saturday and explained that every pass would go over the blue foam stick lying flat across the lane. "It's not goalie practice," Eric said. "It's the opposite of goalie practice. Watch."

He demonstrated the motion he wanted, a soft opening of the blade, the puck rising maybe the height of a shin and then settling. It landed badly twice, then well, then beautifully, dropping flat onto the blade of the next kid in line with a small clean click. A girl near the back raised her hand, the way kids do when they already know the answer. "My cousin does that. It's called a saucer pass." "A saucer pass," Eric agreed, and made her explain it to the line, because she said it better than he could have: the puck lifts just off the ice, flies flat over an opponent's stick, lands right on the receiver's blade. Flat like a saucer, spinning level, never wobbling end over end. The word saucer, she added, was exactly the word's etymology, since the puck sailed flat like the dish it was named for, and Eric decided on the spot that she would someday run this clinic.

For twenty minutes it was chaos, then it was less chaos. The blue foam stick got cleared maybe once in ten tries at first, then once in four. Luis was the worst of them and the loudest about it, his saucer passes knuckling into the boards until Eric knelt beside him and moved his bottom hand two inches down the shaft. The next one skimmed the foam stick, dead flat, and landed on the tape of the kid at the far cone, and Luis stood very still, savoring it, before shouting "AGAIN" loud enough to reach the track.

Afterward Mr. Castillo came down from the warm room with his coffee and watched the last five minutes without a word, which Eric was learning was his version of applause. "Games tomorrow," Mr. Castillo said at the end. "Let's see if it survives contact." Eric tried to assuage his own nerves with the memory of Luis's flat saucer, the click of it landing, but he honestly didn't know yet whether a drill practiced against foam would hold up against actual gleeful defenders, and he told Christopher so at the gate. "We'll find out," Christopher said. "Bring two coffees. One's for Luis. He's captain now, he just doesn't know it yet." Behind them Luis was on the ice, alone, setting the foam stick down and squaring up to it again.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
The card catalog smelled of dust and pencil shavings, and Mia had been staring at it for ten minutes before she understood what it was. Her grandfather's study ran the length of the upstairs hallway, and along one wall stood a bank of small oak drawers, each fitted with a brass handle, each drawer holding hundreds of index cards. On the cards he had recorded, in a small meticulous hand, every book he had read since 1963: title, author, the date he finished it, a single sentence of what he thought. She had come to the house for the quiet, a weekend before her summer course started, and she had brought her laptop with its practice problems. The first problem was the one she had failed twice already: write a binary search, and be able to say why it beat a linear search when the data was sorted.

She had been trying to learn it the way she learned most things, by compartmentalizing, filing the new idea in its own drawer away from everything else, and the filing was not working. The pseudocode sat on her screen and refused to become anything she could feel. So when she found the catalog, she pulled the drawer marked H through K and slid it open, and there they were, hundreds of cards standing on edge in strict order, Hill, Hitchens, Hoban, and she thought: it is sorted. She chose a card in her mind, Hoban, and instead of flipping through from the front she put her finger on the middle of the drawer, looked at the name there, and cut the remaining cards in half with one glance. Then half again. Hoban's card was in her hand before she had counted ten cards.

"You're grinning at my books," her grandfather said from the doorway. He was carrying a lump of speckled stone that he set on the desk, the newest addition to the row of rocks he kept along the windowsill, the igneous ones with their frozen bubbles always at the end nearest the light.

"Binary search," she said. "That's what I just did. You go to the middle, and half the drawer disappears."

He tapped the drawer with one knuckle. "Forty years of alphabetizing."

Her phone buzzed on the desk. It was Eliam, three messages in a row, the way he always wrote when he was panicking. The competition deadline was tomorrow at noon, and their program had to find one student record in a list of eleven thousand names, and Elodie wanted to sort the whole list first so they could run binary search on it, the way the textbook chapter had ended, and she had already started writing the sort. Eliam thought it was a waste of time but could not say why, and he wanted Mia to settle it before Elodie got further in.

Mia sat down on the floor of the study with the phone in both hands. She typed that binary search was faster on sorted data, sure, that was the whole point, she had just felt it happen in the drawer, one glance cutting hundreds of cards to dozens. Then she stopped typing, because she was looking at the drawer, still open, and at her grandfather's forty years of alphabetizing, and a question opened in her that she could not close: how much of the speed came from the searching, and how much of it was paid for earlier, by somebody doing the sorting?

She said it out loud to the room, slowly, testing it. "Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search." Her grandfather, sorting his new rock into its place at the end of the row, did not answer; he had stopped answering questions halfway through her childhood and started just listening, which was its own kind of gift. She pulled a card at random, Angelou, and put it back in the A drawer, and then imagined the whole cabinet unsorted, ten thousand cards in random order, and imagined finding Angelou by going through them one at a time. Long. Then she imagined sorting them first, all ten thousand, card by card into place, before looking for the one name. She looked from the unsorted pile in her mind to the sorted drawers on the wall, and the comparison settled into her with the weight of something physical. Sorting paid off only when the same data would be searched many times. Once you had a catalog like this, looked into again and again across years, the alphabetizing was worth it. For one single search, on a list you would touch once and never again, the sort was a debt you took on for a purchase you would make only one time.

She called Eliam. "Don't sort it."

"It's faster," he said. "You told us last week binary search was faster."

"On sorted data, and only if you already have it sorted. Elodie's sort costs more than one linear search does. We're searching once, tomorrow, and then we're done with the list. It only pays off if you search the same data a lot of times. Tell her to stop."

There was a pause, and in it she could hear Elodie's voice in the background, rising, the particular rising of someone who had been writing code for an hour and was being told to delete it. Eliam came back on. "She says real programs sort first."

"Some do," Mia said. "The ones that search the same list over and over." She was pulling the H through K drawer shut as she said it, the brass handle cool under her fingers, and she heard her grandfather laugh once, low, from the windowsill where he was standing with his rocks.

"She wants to talk to you," Eliam said.

Mia looked down the row of drawers, forty years of one man's reading, every card in its place, and thought about what it had cost him to put them there, and how many times he must have opened these drawers to make it worth that. "Put her on," she said, and sat down on the floor, ready to fight.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
story:
The concert hall smelled of dust and lemon polish, and the piano on stage held the light like a held breath. Faith sat in the fourth row with her staff paper on a clipboard, seventeen bars of nothing except the first two, which she had written and crossed out four times since the workshop began. Mr. Zhang had given them ninety minutes and one rule: sixteen bars, melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, playable by the cellist waiting in the wings.

She had the melody in her head. That was the humiliating part. She could sing the whole thing, had sung it into her phone on the bus that morning, but when she tried to put it down, the notes either bunched up or drifted, and the bars refused to come out even. Annika, two seats over, was already on bar eleven, her pencil moving with an ease that made Faith's wrist ache in sympathy. Laurel kept leaning across the aisle to hum Annika's phrases back to her, effusive in that way of hers, hands wide, eyes bright, praising the descent into the minor chord as if it were a sunset.

Faith counted her first bar under her breath. One and two and three and four. She had a quarter note, then another, then a quarter, then a quarter, and it fit, but it galloped where she wanted it to breathe. In her head the opening note was long, spread out, patient. She tried a half note at the start, then a quarter after it, and the bar came out one beat short. She counted again, tapping her pencil against the clipboard, and got the same starvation, the same hole at the end where a beat should have been.

She flashed back to the theory workbook she'd stolen from her brother's shelf last spring, the one with the coffee ring on the cover. She had read it at the kitchen table while her mother cooked, and there had been a page with notes wearing small dots after their heads, like beauty marks. She remembered being annoyed by them, the way she was annoyed by anything that made her feel behind. She hadn't read that chapter. She'd skipped to the songs.

Mr. Zhang was walking the rows now, pausing behind shoulders. When he stopped at Annika's page he nodded twice and moved on without a word, which everyone knew was his highest praise. Faith bent over her bar, willing the missing beat to appear. She hummed her opening phrase, slow, and held the first syllable out, and it lasted longer than a half note, that much she knew from the piano at school, where a half note under her finger always felt cut short of what she wanted to say.

She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it, and Mr. Zhang came over. "My bar's a beat short," she said, keeping her voice low. "I want the first note long. Longer than a half note."

"Longer how," he said. Not a question, really. He tapped the empty end of her bar once and walked on, and she stared at the white space as if it had insulted her.

The workbook page came back to her, the dots after the note heads. She turned to the back of her own notebook where she'd copied a table of note values, and there it was, small and unglamorous: a dot after a note adds half the note's value. She looked at her half note. Half of its value was one beat. Two beats plus one beat. She drew the dot, small and decisive, right after the note head, and counted the bar. One and two and three and four, and the bar closed like a door clicking shut. A dotted half note, she said to herself, testing the words, three beats. The last beat belonged to her quarter note, and the melody breathed exactly the way it had on the bus.

She filled in the chord letters under the staff, F then D minor, and let the melody fall through them. Around her the hall had gone quiet in the way it did when people stopped performing effort and started working. Laurel had stopped praising Annika and was erasing something of her own, frowning. Faith almost said something to her, almost tried to verbalize what she'd found, but she knew how it would sound, so she slid her notebook with the value table sideways along the row instead, open to the dots, and Laurel looked at it, then at her own page, and gave a small nod without looking up.

When Mr. Zhang called time, Annika played hers first, and it was lovely and clean and finished, and the cellist sight-read it without a stumble. Then he read Faith's, and the opening dotted half note rang out across the empty hall, long and full, and the sound reached the back wall and came back to her changed by the space, warmer. The etiology of the whole piece, she thought, was that one decision, that dot; everything after it descended from the extra beat. Whether the piece was any good she still couldn't say, and she didn't try to. She listened until the last chord faded, pencil still in her hand, and the cellist turned around in his chair.

"Bar fourteen," he said. "Do that again, but slower."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream, a flow oceanographers call 30 sverdrups.
story:
Parker spread the current map across the hood of Ryan's car, weighting two corners with sneakers and one with a fistful of wet sand that kept crumbling away. The wind off the beach pulled at the paper's edge, and every time he smoothed it flat the colours seemed to rearrange themselves, the warm ribbon of red and orange running up the Atlantic coast like a vein.

"It's due at nine tomorrow," Noa said, sitting on the car's bumper with her phone in her lap. "Ms. Swampy said if we can't explain why Europe is warm, we fail the unit. That's, what, eleven hours." She said it without drama, which somehow made it worse. Parker traced the red ribbon with one finger, from the tip of Florida, through the straits between Florida and Cuba, up past the Carolinas, and across toward Norway. Somewhere in that tangle, he was supposed to find an argument.

The numbers were the part he could hold onto. He'd found them the night before in a marine science textbook, sitting at the kitchen table while his mother made tea and asked nothing. About thirty million cubic metres of water per second flowed through the Florida Straits. The book had a name for that flow, a unit named after an oceanographer, and Parker had read the paragraph four times, trying to picture thirty million of anything, let alone water, let alone per second. Eventually he'd given up picturing and just memorized, the way he memorized for chemistry, and felt a little ashamed of it.

"How much is thirty million cubic metres," Ryan asked now, leaning over his shoulder, smelling of sunscreen and the hot dogs he'd eaten at the boardwalk. "Like a pool?"

"A hundred million pools," Parker said. "More. I did it on the bus." He looked at the flat grey-green water in front of them, at the waves folding in, at the pelagic birds riding the air over the breakers, out where the water turned dark and the fishing charters went. He thought about the teacher at the aquarium last summer, on the class trip, who had talked about how the ocean sequesters heat the way a forest sequesters carbon, holding energy in its mass and carrying it for thousands of miles before releasing it. He hadn't understood it then. Standing here, with the map flapping under his hands, he almost did. The water didn't look like it was carrying anything. That was the whole problem.

He remembered being eleven, standing in the shallows at this same beach, getting knocked flat by a wave he hadn't seen coming, and his father hauling him up and laughing and saying, you have to watch the water, not the waves. He had thought it was a joke. Now he crouched at the tide line and watched the foam pull back at an angle, not straight out, and he thought: it's moving sideways. It was always moving sideways, the whole ocean sliding along the shore, patient and enormous, and the wave was just the surface of it.

"That unit," Noa said, reading over his shoulder from the notebook he'd propped against the windshield. "Sverdrups. What is that?"

"Thirty million cubic metres per second, that's thirty sverdrups," Parker said. "It's what oceanographers call the flow through the Florida Straits." He said it and felt the sentence settle into place, the way a key turns. Thirty sverdrups through a gap narrower than the state he lived in, all of it sliding north, and the warm water going where the wind and the rotation of the earth pushed it, arriving off Ireland and Norway and England, releasing what it had carried. Lisbon is farther north than New York, the textbook had said, and Lisbon is warm. He'd underlined it twice and not believed it. On the map, the red ribbon bent east and thinned and spread, and Europe sat downstream like Noa sitting at the end of the outflow from the boardwalk drain, warmer than it had any right to be.

"So which part are you actually going to say tomorrow?" Ryan asked. Parker folded the map carefully, shielding it from the wind with his body, and looked at the darkening water. There was a version where he played it safe, the flow, the warmth, the answer, and a version where he told Ms. Swampy he could recite thirty sverdrups without being able to imagine a single one of them, and that the honest explanation was that he trusted the measurement more than his own picture of it. He didn't know yet which one he'd choose. He slid the map into the cardboard tube, and the wind gusted, and the last of the light went off the water like a hand lifting off a table.

"Give me the tube," Noa said, holding out her hand. "You'll crush it on the way back."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The envelope had been thin, and thin, everyone said, could portend anything, though nobody believed it; thin meant no. Ryder read the letter twice on the bench outside the library before he went in, because his house had his mother in it, and his mother had opinions. "We regret," the letter said, in the polite grammar of institutions, "that we are unable to offer you a place in the incoming class at this time." At this time. Below that, in smaller type: waitlist.

He found Casey in the periodicals room, headphones around her neck, a highlighter bleeding yellow through a photocopied article. She pulled one ear free.

"Guess," he said.

"You got in."

"Waitlisted."

Casey set the highlighter down. She had been waitlisted too, back in March, at her top choice, and she had talked about it so much in April that Lindsey had started leaving the room when the word came up. "You know what that means," she said. "It means you wait until May. That's when they go to the waitlist, after people have sent in deposits and they know how many spots are actually open."

"May," Ryder said.

"May," Casey said, and put her earbud back, which was her way of saying she was sorry and also that she couldn't do this twice.

He walked the stacks to cool off, past the oversized art books nobody borrowed, past the study carrels where the fluorescent light buzzed like a trapped insect. He could smell the carpet cleaner and someone's microwave noodles from the staff room. At the public computer by the far window he sat down and logged into his email. There was a message from the other school, the safety, the one with the good engineering program and the campus he had visited once in the rain. The subject line was "Your Next Steps!" and the body was effusive in the way of admissions offices, thick with exclamation points and the word "Congratulations" in bold, and it asked for a deposit by the first of May. Three hundred dollars. Nonrefundable.

His phone buzzed. Lindsey: "Verdict?"

"Waitlisted," he typed. Then, before he could stop himself: "do I pay the deposit at the other one?"

Lindsey's reply took a while, three dots appearing and vanishing like something breathing. "You have to," she wrote. "It's May. The waitlist only moves in May, once the deposits are in and they can count the empty spots. If you don't pay somewhere, you might end up nowhere. My cousin did that."

"So I'm out three hundred either way."

"Unless you get off the waitlist," Lindsey wrote. "Then you're out three hundred and you don't care."

He put the phone face down on the desk. The light through the window made a hard yellow parallelogram on the carpet, and a kid two carrels over was tapping a pencil against a textbook in a rhythm that was almost good, almost a real groove, like a virtuoso who had been told to keep it down. Ryder thought about his father, who would call it insurance. His mother, who would call it giving up. He thought about the deposit page itself, the little boxes, the way a decision could be reduced to a checkbox and sixteen digits.

Ms. Warsame came by with a cart of returns, the wheels squeaking. She had been the librarian here since he was in middle school, and she had watched him apply for a library card with his whole hand on the pen. She saw his screen without seeming to.

"Both my kids did that dance," she said, sliding a book onto the shelf. "One paid, one refused on principle." She squared the spine with one finger. "The one who paid on principle got in off the waitlist anyway. Life is like that." She rolled the cart on before he could ask which one she meant.

He opened the payment page. He typed his name, then his address, then stopped at the card fields and looked out the window at the parking lot, at a sparrow landing on the hood of a grey car, at the May light already stronger than April's. Then he typed the numbers, slow, like signing something, and hit submit, and watched the wheel spin.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The quiz came back on Tuesday with a red 58 circled at the top, and Ms. Lewandowski kept Eva after the bell while the hallway filled and emptied outside. "You can differentiate," she said, sliding the paper across the desk. "Going backward is where you fall apart." Eva looked at the problem she had left blank, the one with the curve and the shaded region, and said nothing, because there was nothing she could say that was not already written in red. "Retake is Friday," Ms. Lewandowski added. "I'd start tonight."

She did not start that night. She sat in the library with Rayna on Wednesday, both of them hunched over the same textbook, and Rayna kept saying "it's the area, just the area," which was exactly what Eva could not make herself believe. An area was a thing you could draw. The curve on the page bent and swooped, and underneath it was blank space, and she could not see how blank space could equal a number you could compute. "You're being doctrinaire about it," Rayna said, poking her pencil at the page. "Everything has to be a formula for you or it doesn't count." Eva said that was unfair, though privately she thought it might be true.

Thursday afternoon her grandmother called. She needed a ride to the clinic in Fairmont for a Friday morning appointment, her eyes being what they were, and Eva said yes before she remembered the retake was Friday afternoon. She told her grandmother she would need to leave the clinic by one. Her grandmother said that was plenty of time, that Fairmont was forty minutes away if the traffic was kind, and that Eva was a good girl for driving her.

On the way up, bored by the radio and the flat fields, Eva found herself watching the speedometer the way she watched everything when a test was coming, as though the numbers themselves owed her something. At the edge of town the needle steadied at 60, and she thought, almost idly, sixty miles an hour, every minute that passes we go another mile. Ten miles in ten minutes. She glanced at the clock on the dash, noted the time, and began, without quite deciding to, to read the needle every minute and write the numbers on the back of a receipt from her grandmother's purse: 60, 60, 58, 55, 52, 50.

"What are you writing, sweetheart?" her grandmother asked.

"Speeds," Eva said. "Every minute."

Her grandmother was quiet for a moment, then said, "Your grandfather did that once, the whole way to Columbus. He had a little notebook. He said he wanted to know how far we'd gone without the odometer telling him." She looked out the window at the fields. "He trusted his own arithmetic more than he trusted the car."

While her grandmother was with the doctor, Eva sat in the waiting room with the receipt flattened on her knee and drew what she had: a row of skinny rectangles, one for each minute, each one as tall as the speed she had read. One mile, then one mile, then fifty-eight sixtieths of a mile, and so on down the list. She added them up and got a little over nine miles for ten minutes. Then she drew the curve through the tops of the rectangles, the curve the needle had actually traced, smooth and falling, and saw that the rectangles only approximated it, catching too little where the curve dipped inside them, too much where it rose above. Skinnier rectangles, she thought. Every thirty seconds. Every ten. The area under the velocity-time graph was the distance traveled, and the distance was what the rectangles were trying to count.

It was Lilah, texting from study hall, who gave her the word she had been missing. Lilah had looked up the retake topics and sent a list, and Eva read it in the parked car while her grandmother buckled her seatbelt: integration, antiderivatives, displacement. Displacement, Eva texted back, what's that. Lilah replied: "Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph." No emoji, no elaboration, just the sentence, and Eva read it three times with the receipt in her other hand. The area under the velocity graph was not just distance for her grandmother's car. It was displacement, in general, for any function of velocity over any interval, and the integral was the machine that computed it. The blank space under the swooping curve in her quiz problem had been a thing you could count all along.

On the drive home she explained it to her grandmother in pieces, feeling her way through each one. If the speedometer reads sixty for an hour, that's sixty miles, that's a rectangle sixty tall and sixty wide. If the speed changes, the top of the rectangle isn't flat anymore, it's the curve, and the area under it is still how far you went. Her grandmother listened with her hands folded in her lap and said, "Your grandfather would have liked you." Eva did not say that she still couldn't see how the algebra produced the number, only that she could see why the number was worth wanting, and that this felt like a different kind of knowing than she was used to. She had spent three years treating mathematics as a set of procedures whose acumen lay in never asking what they were for. The waiting room receipt had circumscribed something for her, drawn a boundary around it, and inside that boundary was a question she could actually hold.

Friday afternoon she sat in Ms. Lewandowski's room with the retake, and the shaded-region problem was there in a slightly different costume. She set up the integral, worked the antiderivative, evaluated at the bounds, and got a number. She checked it against a quick rectangle estimate, fat rectangles, the way she had started in the waiting room, and the two answers were close enough to each other that she believed the exact one. She underlined it twice, which was something she had never done before, and looked up at the window, where the light had gone long and low across the parking lot.

Ms. Lewandowski collected the papers and said, "Better?" and Eva said, "Ask me again when my grandmother gets home."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Agatha Christie's 1926 novel The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer.
story:
Gabriel had claimed the window seat in the reading nook by seven, which was itself a small miracle, because the essay was due at eight the next morning and he had promised his mother he would not do the whole thing at midnight like the last one. The cushion still smelled faintly of the dog, who was not allowed on it and knew perfectly well that he went on it anyway. On his lap lay a battered paperback of The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, bristling with paper clips, and on the floor beside him Noam sat cross-legged with his laptop open, supposedly helping.

"You realize," Noam said, without looking up, "that you're supposed to be analysing the narrator, not committing a second murder on top of the first one."

"I'm rereading the opening chapters," Gabriel said with dignity. "That's the assignment. Where was he hiding the truth?"

"Everywhere. That's the whole trick. Ms. Ito said the book practically picks your pocket while it's smiling at you."

The deadline gave everything a pleasant edge of panic. Ms. Ito wanted eight hundred words on point of view and the reader's trust by first period, and Gabriel had a thesis that had collapsed twice already, once at dinner and once in the shower. The first version had been that Dr Sheppard, the narrator, was simply lying, which Noam had pointed out was like saying water was wet. The second version had been more sophisticated and also wrong in a way Gabriel could not yet name.

Here he paused, because a memory was bothering him. Last spring, Charley had ruined a film for the entire book club by announcing, forty seconds into the trailer, that the narrator was the killer the whole time. Everyone had groaned and thrown popcorn, and Gabriel had spent two weeks refusing to watch it on principle, and then watched it anyway and been genuinely stunned. What had irritated him most, he realized now, was not the spoiler itself but the fact that knowing the ending had not made the film worse. It had made it stranger. He had spent the whole runtime watching the narrator's hands.

"Wait," Gabriel said. He sat up so fast the paperback slid to the floor and the dog, from the hallway, barked on principle. "That's it. Charley didn't ruin it. Knowing made me read differently."

"That sentence does not augur well for your GPA," Noam said, retrieving the book. "Explain."

Gabriel explained, or tried to, flipping pages with more energy than accuracy. The book club was meeting tomorrow, same deadline as the essay, and Charley had sworn that this time he would keep his mouth shut until the end, a vow nobody believed. Gabriel had already reread the first three chapters hunting for the gaps, the places where the narrator's sentences stayed technically honest while the truth slid past them. "Look at this," he said, jabbing a paragraph. "He tells us exactly what he does all evening and then just... skips the part that matters. He narrates around it. He's not lying, he's being circumspect. Which is lying with better manners."

"Put that in the essay and Ms. Ito will weep with joy. Or fail you. One of the two."

"It's a start, though." Gabriel pulled the laptop toward himself and typed the sentence before he could lose it. The problem was the second half. He could see now that Christie's artifice worked only because the narration felt so ordinary, a doctor pottering around a village, and that the reader's trust in the ordinary was the actual weapon. But he couldn't decide whether knowing the trick destroyed the book or completed it. Charley's spoiler had made the film better for him. Would it make the novel better, or had he already spent his one chance at being fooled?

"Text Charley," Noam said. "Ask him if he'd rather be tricked or be right."

Gabriel texted. Charley replied ninety seconds later with a voice memo, because Charley did not believe in typing like a normal person. "Obviously I'd rather be right," Charley's voice said from the phone speaker, tinny and smug. "But also, in that book, the narrator, Dr Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer, so honestly you were never safe to begin with."

"You already broke the vow," Gabriel said into the phone. "It's due tomorrow and you broke it tonight."

"The vow was for the meeting. We're not at the meeting. Loophole." Charley hung up, or the memo just ended; it was impossible to tell with him.

Gabriel looked at the paperback in his lap, at the paper clips marking every place he had caught the narrator being careful, and at the blinking cursor waiting for him to take a position. He typed: The novel does not break the reader's trust so much as reveal what trust was made of all along. Then he deleted "reveal what trust was made of," because it sounded like a fortune cookie, and typed instead: Whether the trick works a second time, on a reader who knows, is a question this essay cannot answer, though the author appears to have bet that it does. He read it twice. It felt honest, which was more than he could say for Dr Sheppard.

"Eleven twenty," Noam said, standing and stretching. "I'm going home before your mother blames me for the light still being on."

Gabriel saved the file twice, the way superstitious people do, set the paperback on the windowsill where the dog would definitely lie on it, and turned off the lamp.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
Alexander had the good seat, the one beside the lamp where he could see both the television and the door, so when Brendon arrived late with salsa and an argument already loaded, Alexander saw it coming before anyone else did.

"It's thirty-two," Brendon said, setting the bowl down on the coffee table without asking. "It's always been thirty-two. Karly's making it up."

Karly, cross-legged on the rug with her plate balanced on a cushion, did not even look up from the screen, where the pre-match studio panel was still dissecting the semifinal. "Forty-eight. I read it three separate times. It's the first World Cup with forty-eight teams."

"That would be chaos," Brendon said. "That's, what, sixteen extra matches minimum. You'd have to run it for a month and a half. You'd incapacitate the whole European club season." He said the word with relish, the way he said most things, as though volume could substitute for evidence.

Alexander had been quietly working through his own question, which was not who was right but why Brendon was so certain. Brendon's certainty was like that, ductile enough to bend around any new fact without ever breaking, without ever admitting it had bent. Alexander's father, in the armchair with the last can of ginger ale, was no help; he kept saying that in his day it was twenty-four teams and that everything after that was dilution, which Alexander suspected was also wrong, or at least not the point.

It was Ms. Bennett who settled the teams question, though she did it without meaning to. She had come over at halftime of the earlier match to return the casserole dish, had stayed for the smell of popcorn, and was now folded into the corner of the sofa with her shoes off, the only adult who treated the room as though it belonged to the teenagers. During a lull in the argument she looked up from her knitting and said, mildly, "Three countries are hosting it this year, aren't they? Canada, Mexico, the United States. My niece in Toronto has not shut up about it since the draw."

The room recalibrated. Karly sat up straighter. "Right. That. And that's why it's forty-eight, it's the first one with forty-eight teams and the first one three countries have hosted. Together. It's not complicated, Brendon."

Brendon opened his mouth, closed it, and reached for a chip. "First time three countries have hosted it," he repeated, slowly, testing the sentence the way you test ice. "Okay. Fine. That's, actually, kind of a big deal. That's historic. I was wrong about a historic thing." He seemed more fascinated than embarrassed, which was one of the things Alexander liked about him, and one of the things that made him exhausting.

What Alexander kept turning over, while the anthems played and his father shushed everyone out of habit, was how the fact reframed his father's complaint. Forty-eight teams was not dilution if you thought of it as three nations pooling their stadiums, their cities, their whole summer; it was something else, an expansion that only worked because three countries had agreed, for once, to be one venue. Whether that made the football better was a separate question, and an open one, and Alexander was honest enough with himself to admit he had no answer. He liked the tidy old version of the tournament, thirty-two teams, one country, and he liked this sprawling three-nation experiment, and he could not make those two likings agree with each other, and maybe he was not supposed to.

"Stop philosophizing at the kickoff," Karly said, nudging his ankle with her toe.

"I'm not philosophizing. I'm watching."

"You're doing the face. The face you do in Ms. Bennett's class when you're three questions deep into something nobody asked."

Ms. Bennett, without looking up from her knitting, said, "I like that face."

The whistle blew. In the ninth minute a midfielder no one at the party could name slipped a pass through three defenders as though the ball had been shown the way in advance, and Brendon was on his feet, salsa abandoned, and even Alexander's father leaned forward in the armchair, and Alexander leaned forward too, still holding both versions of the tournament in his head, waiting to see which one the game would prove true.

Karly punched his arm. "Goal counts either way," she said.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
Brooklyn arrived at the tutoring centre twenty minutes early, which was the point of everything now. She had a folder, a pencil case, and a stack of practice problems she had no intention of working on alone, because alone she kept getting the same wrong answer and couldn't see why. The centre smelled of dry-erase markers and the instant coffee Ms. Smith kept in a jar by the window, and the fluorescent lights hummed at a pitch Brooklyn had learned to stop hearing. She took the table near the bookshelf, the one with the wobbly leg, and spread out her work.

Nathaniel slumped in across from her, dropping his binder like something he wanted to be rid of. "Calculus," he said. "Again." He had failed the first test and needed a pass to keep his scholarship, which everyone knew and nobody said out loud. Brooklyn, who had a tuition bill taped above her desk at home with numbers that seemed to grow when she wasn't looking, slid her own sheet toward the middle of the table. "Check my derivatives," she said. "I'll check yours."

She went down his page first. His handwriting was cramped, his arithmetic mostly fine, and for a while she found nothing. Then she saw the pattern. For x cubed, he had written three x cubed. For x to the fourth, four x to the fourth. Every single one. She tapped the third line. "You multiplied by the power but you left the power alone." He leaned over, frowned, and flipped back two pages in his binder to his class notes, where a formula sat in his teacher's neat hand: the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1. "The power rule," Nathaniel read off the margin, where the teacher had underlined it twice. He looked at his homework. "So the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared." Brooklyn checked his page again, corrected, and he pulled the sheet back and started rewriting, tongue between his teeth.
