Then she came to her own problem, the one that had followed her home all week: a polynomial modelling the height of something, and the instruction to find the maximum. She had the derivative computed, but every x value she tried gave her a graph that refused to peak anywhere sensible. Annabel arrived with two teas, set one down in front of Brooklyn without being asked, and looked over her shoulder. "You set it equal to zero yet?" Brooklyn had not, exactly; she had been staring at the derivative as if it were a message in a language she could only transliterate, sound by sound, without meaning. She set the factored form equal to zero. Two candidate values appeared. She tested each one, and one of them gave a top, a clean highest point, and the other gave a dip. She circled the first number twice.

She remembered then, suddenly and completely, her grandfather's farm in the valley, the summer she was twelve. He had stood at the edge of the low field after the spring flood, scooping up a handful of dark soil and letting it run through his fingers. Alluvial, he called it, the good dirt the river left behind, and he said the flood was a bad thing that made a good thing, and that you had to wait a season to see which it had been. She had thought he was just being a farmer about it. Now she thought about how the whole field sloped, and how there was exactly one high spot where the water first slowed, and how if you wanted to find it you could walk the slope or you could just know where the rise stopped rising. She kept that thought to herself and wrote her answer in the box, underlined, in pencil.

Ms. Smith came by to collect the whiteboard erasers and paused at their table. "Getting somewhere?" she asked. Brooklyn slid the page over, and Ms. Smith looked for four or five seconds, long enough for Brooklyn's stomach to tighten, then said, "Nice work," and moved on. She was not effusive. Brooklyn suspected the job was close to a sinecure for her, since half the students at the centre were self-teaching anyway out of desperation, and she mostly kept the lights on and the jar of coffee full. Still, the two words landed somewhere in Brooklyn's chest and stayed there.

"Same time Thursday?" Nathaniel asked, packing up. His page of corrections was neat now, the powers all lowered where they should have been, and he had finished the maximum problem on his own sheet while she wasn't watching, getting it right without announcing it. That was the most Nathaniel thing possible.

"Thursday," Brooklyn said. She copied her circled answer onto a clean index card, then copied it again on the back, the way her grandfather had once copied the river gauge readings into his ledger twice, in case of ink smudging. She put the card in her shirt pocket, where she could feel its edge against her collarbone when she stood up. Outside, the parking lot was filling with late-afternoon light, and Annabel was already at the car, waving her keys.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The line outside the community hall moved in small, patient shuffles, and David stood in it with his voter registration card sweating lightly against his palm. He had turned eighteen in March, three weeks after the writ dropped, and had spent the weeks since carrying the card from jacket to jacket like a passport he was afraid of losing. Behind him, Lyra was reading a candidate's flyer aloud in a low voice, eulogizing the man's thirty years of service as though she were speaking over a casket, which, given the polls, she very nearly was.

"He'll lose," she said, folding the flyer into quarters. "Everyone keeps saying it, like it's already happened."

"You don't know that," David said, though he mostly believed it too.

Justina joined the line a few minutes later with wet hair and no coat, having run the four blocks from the pool where she coached little kids on Saturdays. She worked her hands into her sleeves and leaned between them. "Did you two decide? Actually decide, I mean, or are you both still doing that thing where you say you're undecided because it sounds thoughtful."

David had been doing exactly that thing. At home, his father argued at the kitchen table about the economy, waving a butter knife, while his grandfather, on speakerphone from Kamloops, talked about the candidate who had promised an indemnity for the mill workers who lost their jobs the year David started kindergarten. David had listened to both of them for a month, and what he had ended up with was not a decision but a kind of double vision, his father's numbers and his grandfather's faces laid over each other, neither quite cancelling the other out.

Inside the hall, the smell was floor wax and coffee from the bake-sale table the neighbours had set up by the fire exit. Ms. Aydın, who had taught him Grade Ten geography, was working the registration table in a cardigan the colour of rust, ticking names with a pencil she sharpened between voters. When David gave his name, she looked up and smiled.

"First time," she said, not a question.

"Is it that obvious?"

"You're holding the card like it might break." She slid a ballot toward him, then held it a moment longer. "You know, you'd have had to wait three more years, not so long ago. Canada lowered the federal voting age from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970. Before that, someone your age couldn't have done this at all."

David turned that over while he walked to the cardboard screen. 1970. His grandfather would have been twenty-two that year, just old enough under the old rule and suddenly, unremarkably, ordinary. David had assumed eighteen was simply the number, the way gravity is simply down. It had been decided by people, in a year, in a room somewhere. He stood behind the screen longer than he meant to, pencil hovering, the ballot's white surface catching the fluorescent light.

The choices were printed in neat rows. One candidate's flyer, which Justina had passed to him in line, featured a photograph of a montane valley, mist in the pines, and a promise to protect it, though the fine print about how was fine indeed. Another promised the compensation his grandfather wanted, though the flyer in his father's kitchen drawer had a column of figures proving it couldn't be paid. Lyra's doomed incumbent had served on the school board, the hospital board, the hall committee that had, in fact, renovated the very floor David was standing on. He thought of his father's butter knife and his grandfather's voice on the speakerphone and understood, suddenly, that he was not going to resolve them tonight, that a ballot was not an answer but a weight, and that all he could do was place the weight where it seemed most honest to place it.

He marked the paper, folded it, and fed it into the box. The machine swallowed it with a soft mechanical click, and that was all, no bell, no ceremony. Justina went next, then Lyra, and the three of them drifted toward the bake-sale table, where a woman was boxing the last of the oatmeal cookies.

"Polls close at eight," Lyra said, checking her phone. "An hour yet. People are still coming."

Outside, the evening had turned cool, and across the parking lot a man was taping a last sign to a lamp post while his kid held the tape. Justina pulled her coat from her bag at last, and David stood with his hands in his pockets, thinking that somewhere in that box his folded paper was lying under a hundred others, indistinguishable, which was either the whole point or a small grief, he couldn't tell which.

"So," Justina said, tearing her cookie in half. "Did you actually decide, or did you close your eyes and mark one?"

"I decided," David said. Then, after a moment, "Ask me on Thursday why, and I'll have an answer. Right now I just have the pencil mark."

Lyra laughed, and the three of them started across the lot toward the bus stop, the hall's windows glowing yellow behind them, the line inside still moving.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1.
story:
Oliver had claimed the table by the windows before anyone else arrived, spreading his notebook open to the page where he had been copying integrals all week. The school library smelled of carpet and old glue, and outside the glass the October light was going long and yellow across the parking lot. Dominik dropped into the chair across from him with a worksheet, and Valerie came a minute later with two cartons of chocolate milk, sliding one across the table without being asked.

"The area under this curve," Dominik said, tapping his pencil against the paper. "From zero to two. He said it's on Monday's quiz." He had written x to the second, x to the fifth, half of x to the sixth, and beside each one the antiderivative, each term bumped up a power and divided by the new power. Oliver watched him work, because watching Dominik work was how Oliver had learned most of what he knew this term. Then Dominik reached the last problem, wrote one over x, and stopped.

"You just do it the same way," Oliver said. "Bump it up, divide by the new power."

"Watch," Dominik said, and Oliver watched, and somewhere in the middle of it the pencil slowed. One over x was x to the negative one, and if you raised it to the zero power you got one, and if you divided by the new power you were dividing by zero. Dominik sat back. The window ticked as it cooled. "That's not an answer," he said. "That's a hole."

Oliver pulled the worksheet toward himself and tried it a second way, writing the rule out in words so he could see it whole: x to the power n becomes x to the power n plus one, divided by n plus one. It worked for every exponent he could test, two and five and negative two and a half. It worked for all of them except this one, and the exception sat on the page like a loose tooth. Valerie leaned over, read it upside down, and said, "So the rule just dies there? At negative one specifically?"

"Not dies," Oliver said slowly. "It just doesn't apply. The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus one, divided by n plus one, for every n except negative one." Saying it aloud made it feel less like a hole and more like a boundary, the way a fence is not a break in the ground but a line drawn on it. He copied the sentence into his notebook and underlined the last four words.

Dominik was already defensive, the way he got when a problem made him look slow in front of Valerie. "Fine, then the quiz is a trick, and I'm going to fail a trick." He crumpled the corner of the worksheet and then smoothed it flat again, because Ms. Visser was shelving books three aisles over and had already looked at them twice. "Somebody has to know what to do with it."

"Mr. Ferro, maybe," Valerie said, meaning the calculus teacher, who was famous for proselytizing about mathematics to anyone trapped near his door, students, janitors, parents at conferences. Oliver had spent ten minutes of a parent night listening to him compare infinite series to music. He liked the man and he did not want to ask him, because if he asked, the answer would arrive whole and finished, wrapped, and it would never be his.

"I'll figure it out," Oliver said, and Dominik gave him the flat look he reserved for promises he intended to collect on.

That night Oliver wrote to his cousin, who was in second-year engineering and had once mailed him a postcard consisting entirely of a drawing of a sine wave. He kept the letter short, because he did not want to be told the answer, only nudged.

"I learned the power rule for integrals," he wrote. "It covers everything I've tried except one thing, one over x, where it divides by zero. I'm not asking you for the answer. I want to know if the exception means the rule is wrong, or if it means there's a different rule hiding behind it. Is a rule with one exception still a rule? Don't just tell me. Give me a direction to walk in, like Ms. Visser says."

The reply came Thursday, and Oliver read it in the library before math club, at the same window table, while Dominik and Valerie watched him read it, which he found he did not mind.

"Walk toward the number e," his cousin had written. "Take small steps. Think about what grows without ever compounding all at once. And to answer your question: the rule isn't wrong. The rule is a house with one door that opens onto a different house. You'll see." Below that was a single drawing, the letter e wearing what might have been a crown.

"Different house," Valerie said when he passed it over. "That's not an answer either."

"It's more of an answer than we had," Oliver said. He took out his notebook and started a fresh page, and at the top he wrote the exception again, negative one, alone, the one exponent the rule would never touch. He had spent a week thinking mathematics was ductile, something you could bend into whatever shape the problem required, and now he understood it was more like a map with a country the mapmaker had refused to draw, not out of laziness but because the country was genuinely not like the others. Dominik copied the exception onto his own worksheet in careful letters, and Valerie started a list on the back of her milk carton.

Ms. Visser passed their table with a stack of returns and paused, reading the page upside down with the practiced ease of someone who had supervised twenty years of math club. She did not say anything. She set one book down at the edge of the table, a thick one with a cracked spine, and walked on toward the front desk. Oliver turned it over and read the title, then opened it to the index and ran his finger down the column until it stopped.

"There it is," he said. "Page three twelve."

Dominik pulled his chair around, and the three of them bent over the book together, heads nearly touching above the page.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
Grandmother's kitchen smelled of cardamom and dish soap, and Savannah told herself, for the third time that afternoon, that she was not nervous. She had merely come to sequester herself somewhere quiet, away from her brothers and the washing machine and the phone that kept lighting up, so that she could prepare for her interview at Hendrick's Pharmacy in an atmosphere of professional calm. That she had also brought three drafts of answers, a water bottle she kept forgetting to drink from, and a list of possible questions written in increasingly cramped handwriting suggested something other than calm, but she chose not to examine that.

"What time tomorrow?" her grandmother asked, laying two cups of tea on the table with the unhurried precision of someone who had been setting down cups for sixty years.

"Ten thirty. Mr. Patel said to come ten minutes early." Mr. Patel was the pharmacist, a family friend of her grandmother's, which was either an advantage or a trap; Savannah could not decide which. She spread her notes across the table like an affidavit of her own seriousness, as if the pages could testify that she was prepared.

Her grandmother looked at the papers for a while, then reached across and shook Savannah's hand. The gesture was so sudden that Savannah laughed, a short startled sound, before she understood it was an audition. The grip was dry and steady, the kind that had carried laundry and a life across two countries.

"You shake like a fish," her grandmother said, not unkindly. "You apologize with your hand before your mouth can say anything."

"I do not." Savannah shook back, experimentally, and felt her own fingers give way like wet paper. She frowned. "Fine. Show me again."

They practised at the table, then standing, then by the front door, because her grandmother insisted an interview begins at the threshold and not at the desk. On the fourth or fifth attempt, while Savannah was composing what she felt was a genuinely firm handshake, her grandmother mentioned, almost idly, that she had read something in the waiting room of the clinic. A study from 2000, led by a psychologist named William Chaplin, had found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. She said it the way she reported the weather, and went to refill the tea.

Savannah sat with that. She wanted to dismiss it, the way she dismissed the articles Juan sent her at midnight about body language and power poses and the supposed secrets of successful people, most of which struck her as vitriolic nonsense dressed up as science. But this one snagged. Juan had actually mentioned something like it once, in the library, when he was rehearsing for his own interview at the grocery store, and she had rolled her eyes at him. She thought of his face then, the little flicker of embarrassment, and of the way she had been so quick to be superior about a thing she had never had to be desperate about. His family needed his paycheck. Hers did not. That distinction had not seemed to matter at the time, and now it seemed to matter enormously.

Here was the trouble, as she turned her cup in her hands: she did not want to become someone who performed confidence like a costume, who believed that a handshake could stand in for a person. And she did want the job, wanted the register keys and the smock and the after-school hours and the plain fact of being chosen. Perhaps the study was saying something smaller and more honest than the self-help articles. Not that firmness made you better, but that people read your hands whether you meant them to or not, and it cost nothing to decide what your hands would say. She could practise the handshake and still be the person doing the practising. She could not prove that the two things were compatible. She would find out at ten thirty tomorrow.

They ran the whole interview in the living room, her grandmother behind the armchair playing Mr. Patel, asking questions in a voice pitched lower than her own. "Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer." Savannah told the story of the church bake sale and the woman who wanted a refund on a cake she had already eaten half of, and her grandmother laughed so hard she had to stop being Mr. Patel for a full minute. When they finished, the light had gone amber in the window and the cardamom smell had faded to something fainter, like a memory of itself.

At the door, leaving, Savannah put out her hand. Her grandmother took it and held on a moment longer than the exercise required, thumb pressed lightly over her knuckles, the way you hold something you are not ready to put down.

"Your tea went cold," her grandmother said. "You never drink it when you're worried."

"I wasn't worried," said Savannah, and picked up the cup, and drank it all.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
The waiting room of the dental office smelled like fluoride and old magazines, and Alexia had chosen it deliberately, because nobody at school would look for her here. She sat between Antonin and Madalyn with a binder open on her knees, the three of them waiting for Madalyn's little brother to finish his fillings. In forty minutes, when the hygienist called her back for her own cleaning, the rehearsal would be over.

"You're sure the nurse won't think it's weird," Antonin said. "Three sixteen-year-olds asking about IUDs."

"That's the point," Alexia said. "Ms. Munro signed off on it. We're presenting to the ninth graders in June, and if we sound like we're guessing, they'll stop listening in the first five minutes."

The peer health program had been her idea, back in the spring, though she had pitched it in careful language, calling it "wellness education" until Ms. Munro had leaned across her desk and said that euphemisms were how the school had avoided the topic for twenty years. Alexia had liked that. She liked a teacher who refused to be a pedagogue about it, who handed them pamphlets and clinic phone numbers and then got out of the way.

Madalyn pulled the clinic pamphlet out of her backpack and smoothed it on her knee. "Okay, do the whole thing. From the top."

"Consent first," Alexia said. "It's not a form you sign once. It's ongoing, it's specific, and you can take it back at any point, even in the middle." She had practiced the phrasing until it stopped sounding rehearsed, and she watched Antonin's face to see whether it landed. He nodded slowly, the way he did in chemistry when a formula finally made sense.

"Then contraception." Madalyn flipped the pamphlet to the chart. "And here's where I keep messing up the numbers."

"Say it the way the nurse said it to me," Alexia told her. "Hormonal IUDs and the implant fail in fewer than one in a hundred users a year, because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on anyone remembering anything day to day." She had gotten it wrong the first time herself, back in March, when she'd told the nurse she assumed the pill and the IUD were basically the same reliability and the nurse had corrected her without making her feel stupid. That was what Alexia wanted to be, she had decided, not the person with all the answers but the person who made it safe to ask.

Antonin frowned at the chart. "So the difference isn't the medicine. It's that one depends on you every single morning."

"Right. And that's not a character flaw thing," Madalyn said. "It's just real life. People forget things when they're stressed or traveling or seventeen."

"That's the part I want to get right," Alexia said. "Not just the methods but the part where nobody's shamed for how they live." She paused, then said the thing she had been circling for weeks. "I still don't know how to talk about testing without making it sound like a punishment. Like getting tested means you did something wrong."

The receptionist glanced over, and Alexia lowered her voice. "The nurse said you can walk into the clinic and ask, that it's routine, some people go once a year like a checkup. But when I stood in front of the mirror practicing, I heard how my voice dropped on that part. Like it was a secret."

"Then don't drop your voice," Antonin said. "Say it like you said the IUD numbers. Like it's just true."

Madalyn's brother came out then, one cheek swollen, gripping his mother's sleeve, and while Madalyn went to deal with him, Alexia closed the binder and thought about her cousin, who at nineteen had driven two towns over for a test because she didn't want anyone at the local clinic to recognize her. Alexia had thought that was reasonable at the time. Now she thought it was reasonable and wrong, both at once, and she hadn't figured out how to hold those together, whether the answer was more clinics or braver people or just the slow work of making the topic ordinary.

"Alexia," the hygienist called from the doorway, and she stood, tucking the binder under her arm.

In the chair, with the light blinding her and the hygienist's gloved fingers peeling back her lip, she kept going over it in her head. Consent, contraception, testing, delivered as facts rather than warnings. When the hygienist stepped away to adjust the X-ray arm, Alexia said, to the ceiling, "How often do people come in here and lie about flossing?"

The hygienist laughed. "Every other patient, minimum."

"And you don't lecture them."

"I tell them what to do and let them do it," the hygienist said, snapping on a fresh glove. "Rinse, please."

Alexia rinsed, spat, and thought: that, exactly that, except with clinics. When she came back out, Madalyn was waiting with the pamphlet held up like a cue card, and Alexia took a breath and began, right there, with the taste of mint still sharp on her teeth, "Consent first. It's not a form you sign once."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Grace arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided to treat as a fact about the summer heat rather than about herself, and stood at the counter of the shop studying the flavors as though they required scholarship. The boy from her chemistry class, the one whose name she had known for a year without ever using it in a sentence, had asked her out on Wednesday with the specific nervousness of someone reading from a script he'd rehearsed in the shower. She ordered a cone of pistachio and took the window table, where the sun had baked the seat into something nearly igneous, so that she had to shift and settle before she could sit still.

He came in wearing a shirt with buttons, which she noted and forgave. He ordered vanilla in a cup, and when he sat down across from her the conversation began well and then thinned, the way a stream thins over gravel. They covered the heat, the chemistry final, the fact that the shop's freezer made a sound like a small animal in distress. By the time they had each taken four bites, the silence had acquired weight, and Grace could feel them both performing casualness, which is the least casual thing a person can do.

"Okay," she said finally, wiping pistachio from the heel of her hand. "Montana told me about this thing. A study from 1997, by a guy named Arthur Aron. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk."

He looked at her over his cup. "That's the whole study?"

"That's what Montana said. She read about it after she and Melissa stopped being friends and got obsessed with how people get close." Grace found a napkin and wrote 1 through 12 down the side of it, leaving spaces. "We don't have to do all thirty-six. We're not even strangers, technically. But we could do the harder questions."

He was quiet for a moment, and she watched him decide something. "What's number one?"

She made one up, since she didn't know the real list. "When did you last cry in front of someone?" It came out louder than she intended, and the cashier glanced over.

"That's the first one? There's no warm-up?"

"The point is there's no warm-up. Small talk is the warm-up. That's what we just did for twenty minutes."

He set down his spoon. "In front of someone. My sister's wedding, two years ago, but it doesn't count because everyone was crying." Then, after a bite: "Okay, my turn. What do you want to study that you'd never tell your parents?"

They went back and forth. She confessed she wanted linguistics, that she'd spent a whole weekend once on the morphology of Turkish suffixes, how one word could fold an entire sentence inside itself, and that she'd told her mother it was pre-law because pre-law sounded like a plan. He confessed he'd quit the soccer team not because of his knee, which was the official version, but because he'd stopped being able to make himself care, and that he didn't know yet what to sublimate the caring into, so it just sat in him like weather. She liked that sentence enough to write it on the napkin, and he watched her do it without objecting.

Between questions they laughed at the wrong moments, and once she knocked her cone against the table edge and caught it, and once he answered a question about his father with his eyes on the freezer and she let the silence hold until he finished. The napkin filled. Somewhere around question nine she noticed that she had stopped composing her answers before she said them, that the words were arriving unscreened, and it frightened her a little, the way the study had frightened her when Montana first described it. It suggested closeness was a procedure. Ask the right questions in the right order and intimacy follows, as reliable as a recipe.

But watching him scrape the bottom of his cup, she thought it was also possible the questions weren't doing the work at all. Maybe they were only permission. The study's strangers could have asked each other thirty-six hard questions and stayed strangers; what mattered, maybe, was that both people agreed to answer honestly, and the questions just made the agreement visible. She couldn't decide between the two versions, and she understood that she was on a date constructing hypotheses instead of holding someone's hand, and that this too was a kind of answer about herself.

"Question twelve," he said. "Do you want to get out of here and walk down by the water, and keep going until we run out of questions?"

She folded the napkin along its creases and put it in her pocket, where she could feel its corners against her hip as she gathered her things. "That one's mine," she said. "You just asked it."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
Camille set her fork down because her mother had started again about the debate team, and it was hard to eat and argue at the same table.

"If the school cuts the program," her mother said, ladling rice, "that's the end of it. You're saying the school should just cancel anything that costs money."

Camille heard herself stop chewing. "That's not what I said. I said maybe the travel budget could be trimmed. Travel. Not the program."

"Same thing."

"It's not the same thing, though." She looked at the window, where the streetlight was coming on, and tried to find the shape of what bothered her. Her mother wasn't answering her. Her mother was answering something louder and clumsier, a version of Camille that wanted to burn the team down, and then winning against that version easily, without ever touching the real thing Camille had said.

She thought about Thursday. In Mr. Yip's class, Ayan had been arguing that standardized tests shouldn't decide funding, and Kason had stood up and said, "So you think we shouldn't measure anything, that all assessment is pointless." Ayan had blinked, thrown, and Camille had raised her hand before she fully knew why. "He didn't say that," she'd said. "He said tests shouldn't decide funding. Those are different claims." Mr. Yip had written a term on the board then, underlined it once: straw man. Attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same. Camille had copied it into her notebook and felt the phrase settle somewhere useful.

Now, at the table, she turned her glass a quarter turn and thought: her mother was doing it too. Not cruelly. Maybe everyone did it, the way a habit becomes endemic, spreading through a family or a classroom until nobody notices it anymore. But noticing felt like a small door opening.

"Mom," she said carefully, "when I said trim the travel budget, did you hear cancel the program?"

Her mother paused with the serving spoon in the air. "You said cuts lead to cuts."

"I said one specific cut. If the travel money were reduced, then the team could still compete locally. If it weren't reduced, then the dues would go up and Ayan's family probably couldn't pay them. But in both cases the team exists. That's the actual choice." She was surprised by how steady her voice came out. The conditionals lined up like plates on a shelf, each one holding a possible world, and she could point at them one at a time.

Her mother set down the spoon. "You sound like your father."

"Is that bad?"

"It's tiring." But there was something almost like interest under it, the way her mother's shoulders dropped half an inch. "So what would you cut, exactly? Delimit it for me. What's in the travel budget?"

Camille reached for her phone, and after dinner she went upstairs and opened a message thread with Ayan, thumbing fast, because she wanted to get it down before the feeling of the argument dissolved.

I keep thinking about Kason on Thursday, she typed. My mom did the same thing tonight. I told her one small thing and she argued against a huge thing. Is there a word for wanting to win more than wanting to know?

Ayan's reply came while she was brushing her teeth. Probably. People study this for a living. But here's what I keep wondering: does it count as the same fallacy if the person genuinely heard it wrong? Like if Kason really believed that's what I said?

Camille sat on the edge of her bed with the toothbrush still in her hand. That was the question, actually, the one that kept her from feeling entirely righteous. She had assumed her mother was distorting on purpose, assuming an advantage, but maybe her mother had honestly heard trim the budget as cancel everything, the way water finds the lowest crack. Intent was the line between lying and mishearing, and Camille couldn't see it from where she sat.

She typed back: I don't know. Maybe it only matters what you do after. If I say "that's not what I said" and they keep going, then they're choosing the weak version. If they stop, maybe it was just noise.

The three dots appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. Come to practice tomorrow, Ayan wrote. Kason's doing the rebuttal round. You could... I don't know. Watch.

Camille put the phone face down on the nightstand and lay looking at the ceiling, listening to her mother wash dishes downstairs, the faucet running, a plate set in the rack. In the morning she would find Kason before the round started. She didn't have a speech prepared, only a question, which felt both thinner and more honest than a speech: not an answer, but a door held open to see who would walk through it.

At practice, she stood near the doorway of Mr. Yip's room while Kason flipped through his notes at the front. He looked up and caught her watching, and after a second he closed the folder.

"You still think I argued wrong on Thursday," he said.

"I think you argued with something nobody said," Camille said. "I'm curious what happens if you argue with Ayan instead."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Kevin had the chicken out of its plastic wrap before anyone could stop him, and he was halfway to the sink when Jordyn grabbed his wrist.

"Don't," she said. "Don't rinse it."

"My grandma always rinses it," Kevin said. "Every Sunday, my whole life."

They were alone in the kitchen, or nearly; Ciara was out on the porch shelling peas, and Grandma Dozier herself was asleep in her chair, the television murmuring something lugubrious about the weather. Kevin had volunteered to cook the whole dinner this time, chicken and rice and the cabbage she liked, because her hands had gotten slow and because he wanted, privately, to prove that he could hold the shape of her kitchen in his own two hands. He'd stood at that sink since he was six, on a stepstool, watching her hold each piece under the tap.

"The CDC advises against washing raw chicken," Jordyn said. She let go of his wrist. "The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the counters. Everything around it."

"You're making that up."

"Look it up yourself." She slid her phone across the counter, and there it was, the same sentence, on a page that looked official enough that even his suspicion had nowhere to stand. He read it twice. In his head he could see the spray, the fine mist going where he couldn't watch it, onto the cutting board, onto the dish rack, onto the handle of the drawer where Grandma kept her good spoons.

"She's going to say I did it wrong," he said. "She'll come in here and the first thing she'll do is look at the sink."

"So let her look."

That was the problem, though, and Jordyn knew it without him having to say it. Grandma Dozier did not accept corrections. She had opinions about the government the way other people had opinions about neighbors, and any official anything was, in her telling, written by populists or by people who denigrated everything her generation had ever done right. Last summer a man at her church had told her that seatbelt laws were a scheme, and she'd repeated it at dinner for a week. If Kevin stood in her kitchen and told her the CDC said her chicken was wrong, he would not be telling her about chicken at all. He would be telling her that the world had moved on without her, and that her grandson had chosen the world's side.

He put the chicken down on the board. Then he picked it up again, because he heard the chair in the other room creak.

"You drying it?" Grandma asked from the doorway. She had her glasses on and her cane in her hand.

"No, ma'am. Patting it dry for the pan."

"You didn't wash it."

Jordyn opened her mouth, and Kevin cut his eyes at her, fast, and she closed it. He kept his hands moving, salt, then the paprika she kept in the old tin with the faded label.

"I read that rinsing it splashes water all over the sink and the counter," he said. He said it to the chicken, not to her, the way you'd say something you weren't sure was worth a fight. "That it does more harm than good."

He felt her standing there longer than she needed to. The fan above the stove ticked. Then she crossed the kitchen, and he thought, here it comes, but she went past him to the window over the sink and looked out at the pecan tree for a while, at Ciara shelling peas on the porch steps below it.

"Your grandfather washed it," she said finally. "Fifty years, and nobody died."

"Yes, ma'am."

"But I expect more people got sick than anybody counted." She tapped her cane once against the linoleum. "Seems like half of what I was taught turned out backwards." She turned and looked at him directly, which she almost never did when something cost her. "You seasoning that or admiring it?"

"Seasoning it."

"Then season it. And don't let it stick."

He laid the pieces skin-down in the hot fat, and the kitchen filled with the sound he'd been chasing all afternoon, the hiss and spit of it. Jordyn handed him the tongs without being asked. On the porch, Ciara looked up at the window as if she'd heard the pan through the glass, and Grandma lowered herself onto the stool by the door and said, "Now that's how your grandfather started it, anyway."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
story:
Brandon had the museum map almost to himself. The ocean hall smelled like floor wax and the faint fishiness of the touch tank down the corridor, and the current chart glowed on the wall in slow animation, red arrows sliding over blue water like something alive under glass. He was supposed to be filling out a worksheet for Ms. Sato's class, but the worksheet had one question he kept circling: explain, in your own words, how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe.

The problem was that the arrows did not go where he expected. He had assumed a warm current would run straight across the Atlantic, like a hose aimed from America at Europe. Instead the red ribbon hugged the coast, thick and bright, and then, off a label he had to squint to read, it swung away from land. Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. That was where it left the United States and turned northeast across the ocean. He read the label twice, then looked back at the ribbon, following it with his finger in the air, careful not to smudge the screen.

"You're blocking the map," Bianka said, arriving beside him with her worksheet rolled into a tube. She unrolled it and flattened it against her knee. "Also you look like you're conducting it."

"Look at where it leaves the coast." He pointed. "Not New York, not Boston. North Carolina. Then it just turns northeast and goes."

Keiran appeared on his other side, chewing the cap of a pen he had bought at the gift shop, a cheap thing with a plastic dinosaur on the end. "So the warm water goes north and Europe gets warm. Worksheet done. Can we see the shark jaw?"

"It's not that simple," Brandon said, though he could not yet say why it wasn't. He thought of his father, who insisted that weather was all wind and sun and had once dismissed a documentary about currents as "liberal oceanography." Brandon had argued back that week, and the argument had ended in a detente, both of them eating dinner in silence, the television murmuring between them. He wanted something better than silence for Christmas. He wanted to be able to explain it so well that the explanation itself did the persuading.

He crouched and read the small text along the bottom of the display. There was a second chart beside the first, showing sea surface temperatures in color, blue to red, and he stood and compared them, stepping back until his heel hit the bench. The warm tongue of red water and the current arrow occupied the same path. Where the arrow bent northeast, the warm color bent with it, thinning as it crossed toward the far side of the map, toward the gray shelf of northern Europe.

"So the warmth travels," he said slowly. "It's carried there. The water leaves us at Hatteras and takes the heat across."

"Us," Bianka repeated, amused. "You've never been to North Carolina."

"I'm claiming it anyway." He copied the shape of the current onto his worksheet freehand, the coast, the bend, the long reach northeast, and labeled the turn with an arrow and the words leaves coast, turns NE. His handwriting was terrible and he knew it. Ms. Sato would adjudicate between neatness and correctness when she graded it, and correctness was going to have to win.

Keiran leaned in, dinosaur pen dangling from his mouth. "But wait. Why does Europe stay warm if the water's cooling off the whole way? By the time it gets there it's barely red."

Brandon looked. That was true. The red faded through orange into a lukewarm yellow near Ireland and Norway, and yet the display's headline said, in confident white letters, that this current kept northern Europe milder than other places at the same latitude. He stood in front of the two maps with the question open in him, unwilling to close it with the first answer that came.

"Maybe it doesn't have to stay hot," Bianka offered. "Maybe it just has to be warmer than what's already there. Even lukewarm water, moving, brings more heat than cold water sitting still."

"Maybe," Brandon said. He liked that, but he did not write it down as fact. He wrote it in the margin with a question mark after it, and underneath: the current turns northeast at Cape Hatteras, carries warm water across. That much he had. The rest, the why and the how much, he left honest and blank.

Ms. Sato came through the hall then, her lanyard swinging, counting heads without seeming to. She paused at the touch tank, then at the maps, where the three of them stood in a row like jurors. "Finding what you need?"

"Brandon's having a relationship with the ocean," Keiran said.

"Then let him finish it." She moved on toward the shark jaw, unhurried, and her voice carried back down the hall, telling another group not to tap the glass.

Bianka tapped Brandon's shoulder and pointed at a smaller panel by the doorway, one they had all walked past twice. It showed the same Atlantic in miniature, with a dotted line and a note about the current's path. He went and read it, and it said what the big map had said, that the stream leaves the coast near Cape Hatteras and turns northeast across the Atlantic, and he felt the fact settle in him, twice seen, twice confirmed, still carrying its question mark.

"Ten more minutes," Keiran said around the pen. "Then I'm being obdurate about the shark jaw."

Brandon copied the margin note once more, neater, then looked up at the slow red ribbon still sliding across the glowing wall, patient, crossing the whole dark blue of the Atlantic toward a continent he had never seen. "Okay," he said, and zipped the pencil into his bag. "Show me the jaw."

story:
The waiting room of the dental office smelled like mint and hot paper, and Daniel sat beside his father with the phone flat on his knee, screen dark, because he had promised himself he would not check the pharmacy receipt again. The receipt was in his father's coat pocket anyway, folded twice, with the number printed at the bottom in thin gray ink: 125 over 78. His father had tested himself on a whim at the drugstore while Daniel hunted for toothpaste, and then had said nothing about it until they were in the car, at which point he said only, "Probably the machine."

Daniel had spent the evening before at Quentin's kitchen table, where Quentin's mother kept a blood pressure cuff because Quentin's grandfather had moved in with them that spring. She had shown Daniel how to slide the cuff up the arm, how to keep the feet flat and the back supported, how the machine hissed and gripped and then let go. Quentin had filmed the little screen with his phone and made Daniel read the numbers aloud until he could do it without hesitating, systolic first, then diastolic, the top number and the bottom. "You're going to be one of those people who knows things," Quentin had said, in the tone he used when he meant it as a compliment and a complaint at once. Daniel hadn't argued. He wanted, more than he could comfortably admit, to be useful to his father in some way that didn't involve carrying groceries.

The hygienist, whose name tag said Ms. Whitaker, called his father's name at a quarter past four. His father stood, then paused, one hand on the arm of the chair.

"Actually," he said, "the dentist mentioned last time I should have my pressure taken. Would that be today?"

Ms. Whitaker looked at the chart, then at him, then nodded and led them both back. She wrapped the cuff on while making small talk about a nephew's graduation, and Daniel watched the numbers climb and settle, watching his father's face stay carefully quiescent, arranged into calm, which Daniel had learned was a thing people did when they were worried about being worried. The screen read 126 over 77.

"Bit high," his father said.

"Let's see what the guideline says," Ms. Whitaker said. She tapped the tablet twice and then handed it across to Daniel, of all people, as if she'd noticed who in the room had been leaning forward. "You're quicker at this than I am."

Daniel typed carefully. He found a clinic page, then another, and cross-checked them the way Quentin had taught him to cross-check anything, one source being rumor and two being arbitration. The categories came up in a table. Under the 2017 American guideline, a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic below 80 was its own category, not high, not normal, sitting between.

"It's called elevated," Daniel said. He kept his voice level. "That's the word for it."

"Meaning what, exactly?" his father asked.

"Meaning this number, this one time, in a dental chair, after you drove here in traffic." Daniel looked at the screen again so he wouldn't have to look at his father. He understood, in a way he hadn't an hour ago, that the same number could be a fact and an accusation depending on who said it, and that his father had spent the whole drive braced for someone to impugn his habits, his weight, his whole way of living, in a number's small handwriting. "Pharmacy machine said 125 over 78. This said 126 over 77. That's the same reading twice."

Ms. Whitaker wrote something on the chart and said the dentist would talk about follow-ups, and then she left them alone with the tablet, which was kind of her, Daniel thought, because it let his father ask the next question without an audience beyond family.

"So I change things," his father said. It wasn't quite a question. "Walk more. Cut the salt."

"Quentin's grandpa walks with him every morning now," Daniel said. "You could come. He'd like that, and you'd like that, even if you pretend you don't." He was aware of holding two ideas at once and not being able to flatten either one: that his father's body was telling them something and deserved to be answered, and that a number from a chair in a mint-smelling office couldn't be trusted to say everything. He didn't know yet how much the walking would move the number, or in what time, and he said so. "I don't know how fast it changes. We'd have to take it again and see."

His father was quiet for a moment, thumbing the edge of the folded receipt, which he had apparently carried in with him after all. Then he said, "Six thirty too early?"

"Six thirty's fine," Daniel said. He pulled up the pharmacy's number of the machine model and started a note in his phone titled, after a second's thought, Dad, and under it he typed the reading, and the date, and the word elevated, and left the next line blank.
